records.title: Gravity kernels: isolated FFTs and a periodic slab
records.section: Gravity kernels: isolated FFTs and a periodic slab
records.text:
The boundary condition is part of a Poisson solver’s definition. A finite isolated mass, a fully periodic density contrast, and a horizontally periodic disk with vacuum above and below have different Green functions. Padding an array does not by itself choose the right one.
The isolated construction here follows the Hockney–Eastwood doubled-domain convolution idea in Computer Simulation Using Particles. The disk reference is Koyama and Ostriker (2009), ApJ 693, 1316–1345, §2.3 and Appendix A (author preprint). It uses horizontal periodicity, vertical domain doubling, and mode-dependent image corrections. Below we derive and test kernels with our own explicit transform normalization; the finite sampled DFT and the continuum Fourier coefficient are distinguished.

records.title: Gravity kernels: isolated FFTs and a periodic slab
records.section: Isolated gravity: linear convolution on a doubled grid#
records.text:
With G = 1, the three-dimensional isolated potential is
\phi(\boldsymbol x)=-\int\frac{\rho(\boldsymbol x')}{|\boldsymbol x-\boldsymbol x'|}\,d^3x'.
For a source grid Nx × Ny × Nz, pad the density with zeros to 2Nx × 2Ny × 2Nz. Build a kernel using signed grid lags on that doubled domain, multiply its FFT by the padded density FFT, invert, and retain the original physical block:
\phi_{\rm physical}=\Delta V\,
\mathcal R\,\operatorname{IFFT}\bigl[
\operatorname{FFT}(\rho_{\rm padded})\operatorname{FFT}(K_{\rm doubled})\bigr].
Source–target separations inside the retained block are less than the original domain length in each direction. The doubled cyclic convolution therefore equals the desired nonperiodic discrete convolution. This is stronger than merely moving periodic images farther away. Replacing K by the usual periodic symbol −4 pi/k² would solve a different problem.
The singular grid-origin kernel must be declared. isolated_potential assigns an explicit self_kernel, default zero, and uses −1/r elsewhere. It does not integrate the kernel over a finite source cell. Its roundoff-level agreement with a direct grid sum verifies convolution and padding, not high-order continuum accuracy or a uniquely correct self-cell prescription. A fully isolated finite mass can have phi tending to zero at infinity; a slab with nonzero surface density generally cannot.

records.title: Gravity kernels: isolated FFTs and a periodic slab
records.section: Horizontal Fourier transform of a slab#
records.text:
Take x and y periodic and let the density vanish outside a vertical interval of length Lz. With horizontal wavevector k_perp, use the convention
\widehat\rho_{\boldsymbol k}(z)=\frac1{L_xL_y}
\int\rho(x,y,z)e^{-i(k_xx+k_yy)}\,dx\,dy,\qquad
k=\sqrt{k_x^2+k_y^2}.
Poisson’s equation becomes (partial_z²−k²) phi_hat = 4 pi G rho_hat. The full gravitational kernel, including 4 pi G, is
\mathcal G_k(s)=\begin{cases}
-\dfrac{2\pi G}{k}e^{-k|s|},&k>0,\\
2\pi G|s|,&k=0,
\end{cases}\qquad
\widehat\phi_{\boldsymbol k}(z)=\int\mathcal G_k(z-z')\widehat\rho_{\boldsymbol k}(z')\,dz'.
Our sign convention includes the gravitational prefactor in the kernel; some references factor it out. The derivative jump at s = 0 gives 4 pi G, which checks both sign and normalization. Nonzero horizontal modes decay into the exterior. The zero mode is the horizontally averaged mass sheet, with a finite exterior force rather than a decaying potential.

records.title: Gravity kernels: isolated FFTs and a periodic slab
records.section: The vertical Fourier coefficient and the image factor#

records.title: Gravity kernels: isolated FFTs and a periodic slab
records.section: A sampled DFT is a different numerical object#

records.title: Gravity kernels: isolated FFTs and a periodic slab
records.section: Check the boundary physics before a galaxy calculation#
records.text:
import numpy as np
from numart.gravity_boundaries import isolated_potential, slab_potential
rho = np.ones((8,8,16))
phi_slab = slab_potential(rho) # horizontal mean mode retained
phi_isolated = isolated_potential(rho, spacing=(1/8,1/8,1/16))
These two arrays describe different boundary problems. Tests compare isolated FFT convolution with a direct nonperiodic grid sum, including a source near a boundary; verify the mean plane’s quadratic potential and linear interior acceleration; and recover the exponential field of a sinusoidal sheet. For a sheet of surface density Sigma, the mean potential is 2 pi G Sigma |z−z0| and the nonzero mode decays as exp(−k|z−z0|).
The kernel verification manifest records source hashes and measured errors for the displayed checks.
The implementation uses ordinary horizontal periodicity, not shear-periodic remapping. Mass assignment, self-cell integration, vertical quadrature accuracy, force differentiation, and gravity–hydrodynamics coupling require further checks before production use. Continue with particle gravity, multigrid, and Hamiltonian maps.

records.title: Godunov smoothed particle hydrodynamics (GSPH)
records.section: Godunov smoothed particle hydrodynamics (GSPH)
records.text:
Status: source-based reading notes and an implementation plan. The existing
SPH example reconstructs fields; it does not advance a GSPH
fluid. No GSPH benchmark result is claimed here.

records.title: Godunov smoothed particle hydrodynamics (GSPH)
records.section: Inutsuka's formulation#
records.text:
Inutsuka (2002) derives particle
evolution from convolutions of the fluid equations. Pairwise Riemann problems
supply pressure and velocity for the interactions, replacing a separately
prescribed shock artificial viscosity. Riemann dissipation still remains.
The author's preprint, sections 2–3
is the equation reference. It also cites the earlier Godunov-type SPH
contribution (1994); that original report has not been inspected here.
For a common Gaussian smoothing length, a linear approximation to specific
volume V = 1/rho gives the overlap coefficient (equations 48–52)
C_{ij}=\frac{V_i-V_j}{|\mathbf x_i-\mathbf x_j|},\qquad
D_{ij}=\frac{V_i+V_j}{2},\qquad
V_{ij}^{2}(h)=D_{ij}^{2}+\frac{h^2 C_{ij}^{2}}4.
Equation 65 then uses the pair pressure in the momentum update:
\frac{d\mathbf v_i}{dt}
=-2\sum_j m_j P^*_{ij}V_{ij}^{2}(h)
\nabla_i W(\mathbf x_i-\mathbf x_j,\sqrt{2}h).
This is the common-h Gaussian form. The paper's variable-h expressions and
time-centered internal-energy update are needed for its conservation argument.
Changing only the pressure in an existing SPH force is not that derivation.

records.title: Godunov smoothed particle hydrodynamics (GSPH)
records.section: Connecting the existing exhibits#
records.text:
The implementation path joins particle kernels,
Euler Riemann solvers, and moving-particle time integration.
The current interpolation uses a compact cubic kernel; the derivation above
uses a Gaussian and its overlap. Their kernel-width conventions must be kept
explicit. The existing fixed-grid flux returns F(U), whereas a GSPH pair update
needs a consistently oriented star pressure and velocity. Reusing a flux
function alone does not provide a complete particle interaction.

records.title: Godunov smoothed particle hydrodynamics (GSPH)
records.section: A staged verification plan#
records.text:
Check kernel overlaps, specific-volume reconstruction, pair orientation,
equal and unequal masses, and uniform-pressure consistency.
Advance pair forces and internal energy with a matched time update; measure
momentum and total-energy drift before adding adaptive smoothing lengths.
Run a smooth acoustic wave and an advected contact with controlled particle
spacing and smoothing scale. Separate interpolation and time-step refinement.
Compare the paper's first shock tube (equation 89, Figure 2) with its exact
Euler solution, then add the shared Sod and Shu–Osher tests. Record particle
masses, spacing, neighbors, boundary reservoirs, and reconstruction choices.
For that first published shock tube, the primitive left/right states are
(rho, v, p) = (1, 0, 1) and (0.5, 0, 0.2), gamma = 1.4, at t = 0.2.
It differs from the standard Sod parameters used elsewhere in this atlas.
These are proposed verification targets, not computed GSPH results.

records.title: Godunov smoothed particle hydrodynamics (GSPH)
records.section: The MHD branch#
records.text:
Iwasaki and Inutsuka (2011)
extend the particle approach: compressive interactions use a nonlinear Riemann
problem with magnetic pressure, while Alfvén waves use characteristics.
Their paper includes Alfvén, shock-tube,
Orszag–Tang, rotor, and magnetized-blast tests. This is a separate GSPMHD
implementation direction; the atlas's existing grid-based CT/GLM
does not implement it. Particle magnetic-divergence and tensile-instability
treatments would require their own verification.

records.title: Godunov smoothed particle hydrodynamics (GSPH)
records.section: Special-relativistic continuation#
records.text:
Kitajima, Inutsuka, and Seno (2026)
develop SRGSPH with a relativistic Riemann solver, unequal particle baryon
numbers, and variable smoothing lengths. The preprint dates to 2025; the
journal issue is 2026. This is special relativity, not a general-relativistic
fluid solver. Continue with the SRHD/GRHD development review.

records.title: Closed-shell HF for H₂: independent references, SCF residuals and basis refinement
records.section: Closed-shell HF for H₂: independent references, SCF residuals and basis refinement
records.text: Solve two-electron H₂ at fixed proton positions using original s-Gaussian integrals and restricted closed-shell Hartree–Fock (RHF). Energy stabilization, satisfaction of the discrete SCF equations, changes under basis expansion and physical accuracy are separate questions.

records.title: Closed-shell HF for H₂: independent references, SCF residuals and basis refinement
records.section: The model being solved
records.text:
This is a Born–Oppenheimer electronic problem with the internuclear distance R fixed by the input. Atomic units are used: distances in bohr and energies in hartree. Relativistic effects, nuclear motion, vibration/rotation, solvent and periodic boundaries are excluded. Total energy including nuclear repulsion 1/R is recorded separately from electronic energy.
The two electrons occupy the same spatial orbital with opposite spins in closed-shell RHF. The same restriction is retained at stretched geometries. SCF convergence and agreement with another implementation do not establish the correct dissociation limit or recover electron correlation. This is not a switch to UHF, configuration interaction or DFT.
\hat H_{\mathrm{el}}=\sum_{i=1}^{2}\left[-\tfrac12\nabla_i^2-\sum_{A=1}^{2}\frac{1}{|\mathbf r_i-\mathbf R_A|}\right]+\frac{1}{r_{12}},\qquad E_{\mathrm{tot}}=E_{\mathrm{el}}+\frac1R
Sources: Roothaan, C. C. J. (1951), C. A. Coulson and I. Fischer (1949)

records.title: Closed-shell HF for H₂: independent references, SCF residuals and basis refinement
records.section: Gaussian basis functions and original integrals
records.text:
Normalized s-type Gaussians centered on the two nuclei form the basis. A contracted function combines several exponents and coefficients, with normalization also applied to the contraction. Three primitives in STO-3G describe one contracted s function, not three independent basis functions. Inputs and results retain exponents, coefficients and contractions. The STO-3G numerical convention is checked against Basis Set Exchange version 1, rather than presented as a direct transcription of the original paper’s printed digits.
The educational code computes overlap S, kinetic T, nuclear attraction V and electron-repulsion integrals, defining the one-electron matrix as h=T+V. The s-type Coulomb integrals involve the Boys function F₀, which tends to 1 as t approaches zero. Direct evaluation of erf(√t)/√t at zero would produce 0/0, so the limiting region needs a stable treatment. The chemists’ integral index convention and spin-summed density P determine the factor 1/2 in exchange.

records.section: Gaussian basis functions and original integrals
records.text: Sources: Boys, S. F. (1950), Roothaan, C. C. J. (1951), W. J. Hehre, R. F. Stewart and J. A. Pople (1969), Basis Set Exchange (2018)

records.title: Closed-shell HF for H₂: independent references, SCF residuals and basis refinement
records.section: How SCF convergence is judged
records.text:
Symmetric orthogonalization converts the Roothaan equation to an ordinary eigenproblem. Occupied orbitals define a new density, which rebuilds the Fock matrix for the next iteration. Density mixing can stabilize iterations, but an intermediate mixed density need not satisfy the idempotency condition of a pure determinant. Final density, orbitals and Fock matrix are therefore checked in a consistent state.
A small energy change alone is insufficient. Energy change, the Frobenius norm of the AO-density change and the Frobenius norm of the orthonormal-coordinate commutator residual are compared with input thresholds. Orbital orthogonality, electron count Tr(PS)=2 and closed-shell idempotency PSP=2P are also measured. The matrix-trace energy with F[P] rebuilt from the final density is compared with a separate occupied-orbital/electron-repulsion-integral reconstruction.
The minimum overlap eigenvalue and condition number are recorded. Near-linear dependence makes S⁻¹ᐟ² amplify errors. Termination reasons and iteration limits are explicit; reaching the limit is not reported as convergence. A stationary solution also need not be a stable minimum, so residual checks do not replace a full RHF/UHF stability analysis.

Sources: Roothaan, C. C. J. (1951), PySCF developers (2026)

records.title: Closed-shell HF for H₂: independent references, SCF residuals and basis refinement
records.section: Basis refinement and its limits
records.text:
SCF tolerance controls the remaining solution error within one fixed basis. A basis change changes the discrete problem itself. Basis comparisons retain tight SCF settings, geometry, nuclear repulsion and the RHF constraint. True RHF minima in nested variational spaces cannot increase in energy under expansion. Switching to a different local stationary branch would invalidate that simple comparison.
Refinement here is limited to the finite s-only sequence defined by the public input. Adjacent-basis energy changes are measured, but the absence of p and higher angular functions means this does not prove convergence to the complete-basis-set (CBS) limit or chemical accuracy. Unrelated basis sets and different contractions are not all treated as a nested sequence. For each separation, the final two additions are checked against the stated energy-change target. This is a stopping diagnostic for the published sequence, not an upper bound on true basis error.
The tolerance sweep changes only SCF thresholds and compares with a tighter solution. The basis sweep keeps SCF settings aligned. These differences and independent-implementation differences are separate outputs. A small final basis increment does not eliminate physical approximation error.

records.text: THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: Historical atlas
records.text:
Dates refer to original publication years, with translations, reprints, and
online publication dates distinguished where relevant. This atlas offers a
reading path through representative sources. It does not settle every claim
of invention or priority. The reference catalog records the
relationship between each source and the implementation, including open questions.

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: Classical foundations: equations, differences, and iteration#
records.text:
Begin with forward, backward, and centered differences, Euler time integration,
Fourier expansions, heat conduction, and the Laplace and Poisson equations.
Distinguish boundary values from boundary fluxes before introducing Dirichlet,
Neumann, and Robin conditions. The mathematical origins of these ideas precede
their later use in computational fluid dynamics.

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: 1928: CFL and domains of dependence#
records.text:
Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy compares the continuous domain of dependence with the
reach of a discrete stencil. Vary C=a Δt/Δx in linear advection to distinguish
necessary conditions from sufficient ones.
Original CFL paper,
derivations and experiments.

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: 1939–1943: kinetic asymptotics and variational assembly#
records.text:
Chapman–Cowling's kinetic-theory book appeared in 1939; this is a book date,
not the invention date of the Chapman–Enskog expansion.
Courant (1943) connects
variational problems to piecewise representations. The P1 FEM exhibit
implements independent sparse Poisson examples.

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: 1947–1950: diffusion, implicit methods, and linear stability#
records.text:
Crank–Nicolson (1947); Thomas tridiagonal elimination, commonly cited to a 1949
report whose original text has not been inspected here; and stability analysis
in Charney–Fjørtoft–von Neumann's numerical forecasting work (1950).
The 1950 paper is historical context, rather than a claim that von Neumann
analysis originated in that paper alone. Connect the diffusion number
r=ν Δt/Δx² with A-stability, monotonicity, and implicit linear systems.
Diffusion and linear solvers.
Burgers (1948) supplies a
parallel nonlinear model branch. The equation gallery
uses the inviscid shock/fan problem, rather than reproducing its turbulence analysis.

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: 1954–1961: Lax, Godunov, and conservation form#
records.text:
Lax (1954), Lax–Richtmyer (1956), Godunov (1959), Lax–Wendroff (1960), and
Rusanov (1961) lead into weak solutions, numerical fluxes, shock speeds,
numerical viscosity, and dispersion. The Lax–Richtmyer linear convergence
theorem and Lax–Wendroff-type results about weak limits of nonlinear
conservative approximations have different hypotheses.
Here, method="godunov" denotes a Godunov-type finite-volume method with
approximate Riemann fluxes, rather than a complete reproduction of the
original exact-flux algorithm.
BGK (1954) provides a kinetic
relaxation model. Lighthill–Whitham (1955)
and Richards (1956) connect conservation
laws to traffic waves. These separate branches meet in the gallery through
explicit equations and references, not a single invention chronology.

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: 1961–1977: relaxation, multigrid, and local and global bases#
records.text:
Fedorenko (1961), Reed–Hill (1973), Gottlieb–Orszag (1977), and Brandt (1977).
Split Poisson iteration into smoothing of high-frequency errors and coarse-grid
correction of smooth errors. DG uses elementwise polynomials joined by boundary
fluxes; spectral methods use global bases. Earlier Galerkin and Fourier ideas
provide the mathematical background to these developments.
Poisson and multigrid, numart.advection.dg_advection.
Chorin (1968)
leads to incompressible projection.
Alexander (1977) supplies the
SDIRK branch; source treatment and adaptive error control
remain distinct from a method's linear stability function.

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: 1978–1983: shared benchmarks and high-resolution fluxes#
records.text:
Sod (1978), van Leer's MUSCL (1979), Orszag–Tang (1979), Roe (1981), and
Harten–Lax–van Leer (1983). Compare contact and acoustic-wave resolution on the
same Sod problem. The first-edition MUSCL implementation uses minmod and the
method of lines; van Leer's original Lagrangian/remap construction is different.
The original incompressible Orszag–Tang study and the normalization of today's
compressible test are also distinguished.
Benchmark definitions, MHD.

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: 1984–1989: TVD slopes and TVB extrema relaxation#
records.text: Sweby (1984) organizes scalar flux-limiter bounds. Cockburn–Shu (1989) develops the TVB RKDG framework. Compare five slope limiters, then inspect the separate TVB and positive-state scaling building blocks. The latter also links the positivity framework of Zhang–Shu (2010), with its required flux, quadrature, CFL, and SSP conditions.

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: 1985–1991: cubic profiles and transported gradients#
records.text: Takewaki–Nishiguchi–Yabe (1985) and Yabe–Aoki (1991) develop the CIP line of cubic value/gradient transport. The CIP chapter computes a constant-speed scalar example and distinguishes later conservative and rational branches. Its constructed Hermite-field test separates low diffusion from a mass-conservation guarantee.

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: 1987–1989: higher order, preconditioning, and magnetic constraints#
records.text:
ENO by Harten and colleagues (1987), Turkel's low-speed preconditioning (1987),
Einfeldt (1988), Evans–Hawley CT (1988), Shu–Osher (1988, 1989), and
Cockburn–Shu RKDG (1989). High-order interpolation alone does not ensure robust
shock capture. Entropy fixes and positivity require separate attention.
The Shu–Osher test combines a shock with a smooth density wave.

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: 1991–1996: unsteady iteration, low densities, HLLC, and WENO#
records.text:
Einfeldt and colleagues (1991), Jameson (1991), Toro–Spruce–Speares (1994),
Liu–Osher–Chan (1994), and Jiang–Shu (1996). Study physical and pseudo-time,
low-density failure, contact restoration, and nonlinear WENO weights.
The origin of WENO in 1994 is distinguished from WENO5-JS (1996), which is the
variant implemented in this edition.
Preconditioning and dual time stepping.

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: 2000–2008: multidimensional robustness and constraints#
records.text:
Tóth (2000), Dedner and colleagues (2002), Abgrall's residual-distribution
review (2006), and Nishikawa–Kitamura (2008). Follow discrete CT/GLM operators,
conservative residual distribution, rotated-hybrid fluxes, and the carbuncle
instability. The 2006 date identifies the RD review, rather than the invention
of residual distribution.
Inutsuka (2002) adds a parallel
particle branch: convolution-based SPH evolution with pairwise Riemann
problems. The GSPH chapter distinguishes its 1994 precursor from
the detailed 2002 formulation and the later MHD extension by
Iwasaki–Inutsuka (2011).
These are source notes and planned fluid solvers, rather than the existing
static SPH reconstruction.

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: 2001–2009: SSP inheritance and additional Runge–Kutta stages#
records.text: Gottlieb–Shu–Tadmor (2001), Spiteri–Ruuth (2002), and Gottlieb–Ketcheson–Shu (2009) distinguish scalar linear stability from conditional nonlinear stability inheritance. These are developments in the SSP branch, not the origin of Runge–Kutta methods. The RK family chapter compares RK2 variants, RK4, and SSPRK(s,p), with actual nonlinear stages and refinement.

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: Relativistic branch: 1972–2026#
records.text:
The SRHD/GRHD/GRMHD review connects Wilson's
Kerr-background calculation (1972), exact SR Riemann solutions (1994), Valencia
(1997), local-frame solvers (1998), relativistic magnetic constraints, HARM
(2003), dynamical spacetime, and nonlinear primitive recovery. Later branches
include radiation, DG–FD hybrids, physical-state constraints, and GPU-oriented
merger codes. SRGSPH (2026) connects
back to Inutsuka's particle formulation. The review records source and
publication status as checked on 6 November 2026; it adds no relativistic solver.

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: Toward modern verification and validation#
records.text:
The NASA 2D case catalog introduces the distinction between
numerical verification and physical validation against experiments. Each
future exhibit should connect its original source, current data access point,
implementation status, and verification evidence.

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: Moving meshes, particles, and temporal modes#
records.text:
The fixed-grid history has parallel branches. Hirt, Amsden, and Cook (1974) provide a classical ALE framework; Gingold and Monaghan (1977) and Lucy (1977) are independent early SPH sources. The new ALE, particle, and mesh chapters connect their different representations of geometry and motion. The code implements small reconstruction and geometric-conservation examples, rather than those original flow calculations.
The time integration chapter gives the two-step leapfrog recurrence and its computational root. Its discussion of time filtering points to a later modification by Williams (2009), without assigning the invention of leapfrog to that paper.
The Double Mach Reflection exhibit adds a computed two-dimensional shock interaction. Quirk (1994) and Pandolfi and D’Ambrosio (2001) lead into the separate carbuncle reading notes. Finally, Remembering Philip L. Roe records the university’s 2026 memorial and returns to his 1981 contribution.

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: Particle fields and canonical time maps#
records.text: Hockney’s P³M account (1981), Barnes–Hut (1986), and Greengard–Rokhlin (1987) connect mesh, tree, and expansion-based field calculations. Yoshida (1990) provides a route to high-order symplectic compositions. The new gravity and Hamiltonian-map chapters make their different roles explicit. Koyama–Ostriker (2009) supplies the disk-potential FFT reference in the boundary-kernel chapter.

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: Smooth-flow structure and honest test selection#
records.text: Kuya, Totani, and Kawai (2018) introduce the KEEP line of compressible-flow discretizations. The KEEP chapter implements the original second-order Cartesian form and distinguishes later entropy, pressure-equilibrium, and temporal extensions. Its smooth-vortex refinement and saved-state movie are separate from shock-capturing benchmarks; neither kinetic-energy consistency nor a visually smooth movie is a universal stability guarantee.

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: Parallel solver branches: 1986–2010#
records.text:
GMRES (1986) and
BiCGSTAB (1992) provide nonsymmetric
sparse-system solvers.
Qian et al. (1992) and
Guo et al. (2002) lead to the
lattice-BGK and forcing exhibits.
Nishikawa (2007) develops the
first-order hyperbolic diffusion system, with an
advection–diffusion extension published in 2010. The reading room distinguishes
that system's original second-order RD scheme from our first-order FV baseline.

records.title: Historical atlas
records.section: Biological and geophysical branches#
records.text:
The biological equation survey follows population
growth through Lotka/Volterra, age structure and SIR, then Fisher fronts,
Turing morphogenesis, excitable membranes, chemotaxis, stochastic reaction
networks and synthetic gene circuits. Original, translated and reduced model
forms have separate source notes. All 22 biological entries are survey-only.
Arakawa–Lamb (1977)
connects variable placement to geophysical waves. The A/B/C chapter
adds independent centered f-plane symbol comparisons; the horizontal grid
classification is separate from vertical staggering and nonlinear invariant
conservation.
Rotated Riemann sources: Ren (2003), Roe–Nishikawa et al. (2005), Nishikawa–Kitamura (2008) and the atlas experiment

records.title: Nishikawa's hyperbolic diffusion: iterate a first-order system
records.section: Nishikawa's hyperbolic diffusion: iterate a first-order system
records.text:
Hiroaki Nishikawa (2007)
introduces the first-order hyperbolic-system approach to steady diffusion,
including second-order residual-distribution schemes. The
2010 extension unifies advection
and diffusion. The date is the journal publication year, not the DOI's year.
Implemented here: a periodic 1D, first-order upwind finite-volume baseline
with SSPRK2. It demonstrates equivalent steady equations; it does not implement
the original paper's second-order multidimensional RD constructions.

records.title: Nishikawa's hyperbolic diffusion: iterate a first-order system
records.section: Evolve the solution and its gradient#
records.text:
For the steady problem −νu_xx=f, introduce p and pseudo-time τ:
\partial_\tau u-\nu\partial_x p=f,\qquad
\partial_\tau p-\frac1{T_r}\partial_x u=-\frac p{T_r}.
At convergence, p=u_x, recovering the original steady diffusion equation.
The homogeneous flux Jacobian has eigenvalues
\lambda_\pm=\pm\sqrt{\nu/T_r}.
The relaxation time T_r is a numerical parameter controlling pseudo-time
propagation and damping. It is not the physical diffusivity. A hyperbolic
Courant restriction scales with h for fixed T_r; an explicit source treatment
also has a relaxation restriction. The demonstration therefore uses
\Delta\tau=\frac{C}{a/h+1/T_r},\qquad
 a=\sqrt{\nu/T_r},\quad C\leq\frac12.
A physical heat equation is not recovered at every finite pseudo-time.
Replacing the heat gallery's physical-time curve by this iteration history
would change the problem. Time-accurate extensions require additional analysis.

records.title: Nishikawa's hyperbolic diffusion: iterate a first-order system
records.section: Residual convergence and discretization error#
records.text:
The manufactured steady reference is sin(2πx), with zero mean on the periodic
unit interval and forcing ν(2π)²sin(2πx). The initial mean fixes the constant
null mode. Both equation residuals are measured; the gradient residual is
scaled by 2π in the combined RMS diagnostic. A small residual does not eliminate
the first-order upwind spatial error. N=32,64,128 checks that error separately.
The manifest records steps and pseudo-time
sizes, without a matched-cost speedup claim.
Compare Thomas and multigrid, sparse preconditioning,
and the physical diffusion gallery. Anisotropic
diffusion, high-order face reconstruction, viscous Navier–Stokes coupling and
the complete RD formulation are future extensions. Publisher records and
abstracts were checked; full original-paper reproductions are not claimed.

records.title: Incompressible flow: project with compatible discrete operators
records.section: Incompressible flow: project with compatible discrete operators
records.text:
Implemented: unit-density periodic 2D Navier–Stokes on a MAC grid, centered
convection and viscosity, projected SSPRK2, and discrete-FFT Poisson inversion.

records.title: Incompressible flow: project with compatible discrete operators
records.section: 1968: the projection branch#
records.text:
Chorin (1968)
is the original projection reference. Our periodic RK model illustrates the
principle; it does not reproduce his boundary treatments or original time step.
Velocity components live on different faces; pressure lives at cell centers.
Choose divergence D and gradient G so that D=−Gᵀ under the periodic grid
inner product. Then
DG\phi=D\boldsymbol u^*,\qquad
\boldsymbol u=\boldsymbol u^*-G\phi,\qquad D\boldsymbol u=0.
The FFT must invert the symbol of DG, not continuum −|k|²:
\lambda_h=-\frac4{h^2}
\left[\sin^2(k_xh/2)+\sin^2(k_yh/2)\right].
The pressure constant is undetermined. Set its mean to zero; subtract the mean
from the Poisson source for periodic compatibility. Tests check the adjoint
identity, projection idempotence, energy contraction and divergence removal.

records.title: Incompressible flow: project with compatible discrete operators
records.section: Taylor–Green verification#
records.text:
On [0,2π)² with viscosity ν, use
u=\sin x\cos y\,e^{-2\nu t},\qquad
v=-\cos x\sin y\,e^{-2\nu t}.
The velocity error refines at second order for N=16,32,64 at T=0.5, ν=0.1.
Mean kinetic energy is e^(−4νt)/4. Stage projection multipliers are not
silently labeled physical pressure; a final pressure estimate is reconstructed
from the momentum RHS, without a claimed pressure-order verification.
Reproducible measurements include maximum
absolute discrete divergence. The explicit step retains both advective and
viscous restrictions. No-slip cavity boundaries, SIMPLE/PISO, cylinder wakes,
mixed FEM, turbulence models and experimental validation are not implemented
by this periodic test. Compare the separate low-Mach LBM model.
The Arakawa A/B/C comparison places this MAC
arrangement in a geophysical context. Matching face locations does not
automatically supply a Coriolis or potential-vorticity algorithm.

records.title: KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits
records.section: KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits
records.text:
KEEP stands for kinetic-energy and entropy preserving. The work of Yuichi Kuya, Kosuke Totani, and Soshi Kawai at Tohoku University seeks a low-dissipation balance between the conservative equations of compressible flow. The original 2018 paper is the starting point. The authors’ 2022 conference explanation, especially §2.2 and Eq. (9), states the Cartesian flux implemented here.
This exhibit implements the original second-order arithmetic-mean Cartesian flux, with periodic boundaries and classical RK4. It does not implement every later scheme named KEEP. Watch its smooth-vortex evolution.

records.title: KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits
records.section: Which quantities should be preserved?#
records.text:
In a smooth periodic inviscid flow, mass, momentum, and total energy are conservative. The total kinetic energy alone is generally not constant in compressible flow: pressure work exchanges kinetic and internal energy. With K = integral rho |u|²/2,
\frac{dK}{dt}=\int p\,\nabla\cdot u\,dV.
A kinetic-energy-consistent convective discretization should not create a spurious kinetic-energy source through an inconsistent mass/momentum product rule. This is different from imposing dK/dt = 0 on a compressible vortex.
We measure the dimensionless entropy proxy
S_* = \int\rho\log\left(\frac{p}{\rho^\gamma}\right)dV.
For a fixed ideal-gas composition this differs from physical entropy only by fixed factors and an additive mass term. Its change per initial mass is useful when initial isentropic data give S_* approximately zero; dividing by initial S_* would be ill-conditioned.
For the grid update formula, see the semidiscrete update and two-point flux.

records.title: KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits
records.section: The semidiscrete update and two-point flux#
records.text:
Let an overbar denote the arithmetic mean of left and right values, u_n the velocity normal to a Cartesian face, and e = p/[rho(gamma−1)]. The baseline flux is
\begin{aligned}
C&=\overline\rho\,\overline u_n,\\
F_{\rho u_i}&=C\,\overline u_i+\overline p\,\delta_{in},\\
F_E&=C\left[\frac12\boldsymbol u_L\cdot\boldsymbol u_R+\overline e\right]
+\frac12(u_{n,L}p_R+u_{n,R}p_L).
\end{aligned}
The mass flux is C. The cross-velocity kinetic term and cross-pressure work are deliberate; replacing them by a convenient average of the full physical flux changes the discrete energy exchange. The implementation is a central two-point flux-difference method of second spatial order. It has no Riemann-solver dissipation.

records.title: KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits
records.section: 1. Distinguish the two discrete operators#
records.text:
Work first in one space dimension on a periodic uniform grid of spacing h, with positive density. The left and right states at a face are the two neighboring nodal values. A bar is their arithmetic mean and a jump is right minus left. D differences a face flux; D₀ is the centered derivative of a nodal field.
\begin{aligned}\bar a_{i+1/2}&=\frac{a_i+a_{i+1}}2,\qquad [a]_{i+1/2}=a_{i+1}-a_i,\\(D\mathcal F)_i&=\frac{\mathcal F_{i+1/2}-\mathcal F_{i-1/2}}h,\\(D_0a)_i&=\frac{a_{i+1}-a_{i-1}}{2h}.\end{aligned}
Two exact algebraic identities explain why the particular averages matter:
[ab]=\bar a[b]+\bar b[a],\qquad
\overline{ab}=\bar a\,\bar b+\frac14[a][b].
For example, averaging ρu is different from multiplying the separate means of ρ and u. They agree for equal states and to first order about a constant state, but their nonlinear jump terms differ. KEEP chooses the products of means to make the equations exchange energy consistently. Conservation of the summed total energy alone would not determine these products.

records.title: KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits
records.section: 2. Derive kinetic energy from mass and momentum#
records.text:
Let m denote momentum per unit volume. Use the mass flux C and momentum flux M below; each face has one shared flux. The full two-dimensional flux was given above. Here the velocity is a scalar to expose the cancellation.
\begin{aligned}m_i&=\rho_i u_i,\qquad\dot\rho_i=-(DC)_i,\qquad\dot m_i=-(DM)_i,\\C&=\bar\rho\,\bar u,\qquad M=C\bar u+\bar p.\end{aligned}
Time is still continuous, so the ordinary chain rule applies to K=m²/(2ρ). Substituting the two conservative equations gives a kinetic-energy flux 𝒦 and a pressure-gradient term:
\begin{aligned}
K_i&=\frac{m_i^2}{2\rho_i}=\frac12\rho_i u_i^2,\\
\dot K_i&=u_i\dot m_i-\frac12u_i^2\dot\rho_i
=-(D\mathcal K)_i-u_i(D_0p)_i,\\
\mathcal K_{i+1/2}&=\frac12 C_{i+1/2}u_i u_{i+1}.
\end{aligned}
The advective cancellation at the right face is explicit:
u_i\left(C_{i+1/2}\frac{u_i+u_{i+1}}2\right)
-\frac12u_i^2 C_{i+1/2}
=\frac12u_i u_{i+1}C_{i+1/2}.
The left face cancels in the same way. Also D applied to the face mean of p is D₀p. Summing over the periodic grid cancels all shared kinetic-energy fluxes; discrete summation by parts then gives
\frac{d}{dt}\left(h\sum_i K_i\right)
=-h\sum_i u_i(D_0p)_i
=h\sum_i p_i(D_0u)_i.

records.title: KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits
records.section: 2. Derive kinetic energy from mass and momentum#
records.text: The sign is positive in the last expression: pressure dilatation transfers energy between kinetic and internal energy. Thus compressible-flow kinetic energy is generally not constant. The identity excludes a spurious advective source while retaining that physical exchange. In multiple dimensions, replace uLuR by the velocity dot product and sum the directional pressure work.

records.title: KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits
records.section: 3. Recover the internal-energy pressure work#
records.text:
Choose the pressure contribution P to the total-energy flux as a cross product of left and right values. Expanding its face difference gives an exact discrete product rule:
\begin{aligned}
P_{i+1/2}&=\frac12(u_i p_{i+1}+u_{i+1}p_i),\\
(DP)_i&=\frac{u_i(p_{i+1}-p_{i-1})+p_i(u_{i+1}-u_{i-1})}{2h}\\
&=u_i(D_0p)_i+p_i(D_0u)_i.
\end{aligned}
Use the same mass flux to transport the arithmetic mean of the specific internal energy. Subtracting the derived kinetic-energy equation from the total-energy equation then yields
\begin{aligned}
I_i&=\rho_i e_i=E_i-K_i,\qquad e_i=\frac{p_i}{\rho_i(\gamma-1)},\\
\mathcal I_{i+1/2}&=C_{i+1/2}\bar e_{i+1/2},\qquad
F^E=\mathcal K+\mathcal I+P,\\
\dot E_i+(DF^E)_i&=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dot I_i+(D\mathcal I)_i+p_i(D_0u)_i=0.
\end{aligned}
The unwanted uD₀p terms cancel, leaving the internal-energy pressure work pD₀u with the required sign. This explains the cross-pressure term and the cross-velocity kinetic term in the implemented flux. They are not an arbitrary average of the physical energy flux. These are independent algebraic steps for the published implementation, corresponding to the second-order formulation in §2.2, Eqs. (8)–(12).

records.title: KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits
records.section: 3. Recover the internal-energy pressure work#
records.text: This derivation does not prove roundoff-exact entropy conservation. Entropy also involves nonlinear thermodynamic chain rules. The arithmetic-mean 2018 baseline preserves the balances above but retains entropy-conservation error; later KEEP variants and logarithmic-mean entropy-conservative fluxes have different definitions. The next formula returns to the actual two-dimensional update used by the code.

records.title: KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits
records.section: 4. The implemented two-dimensional update
records.text:
Here F(x) and F(y) are the two-point flux above with normal velocity u and v, respectively. In the public numart/keep.py, rhs() forms the right flux with keep_flux(q, np.roll(q, -1, axis=axis), axis) and subtracts the left flux obtained with np.roll(flux, 1, axis=axis). The implementation uses a square periodic uniform grid with Δx = Δy = L/N. This is a nearest-neighbor, second-order central spatial operator; higher-order multi-point assembly and curvilinear forms are not implemented.
Both neighboring nodes share the same face flux. Its differences telescope when summed over the periodic grid, conserving total mass, momentum and total energy. RK4 retains these linear conservation laws, apart from roundoff. Kinetic-energy pressure-work balance and entropy involve nonlinear relations: this spatial formula alone does not guarantee their exact preservation after time discretization.
Tests verify equal-state consistency, left/right symmetry, periodic conservation of the primary variables, and the semidiscrete kinetic-energy pressure-work identity. RK4 adds temporal truncation error and does not inherit every semidiscrete identity exactly.

records.title: KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits
records.section: Non-dissipative does not mean dispersion-free#

records.title: KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits
records.section: Non-dissipative does not mean dispersion-free#
records.text:
The ratio at θ=0 is understood by continuity. At four grid points per wavelength, θ=π/2, the second-order phase speed is only 2/π≈0.637 times a. At θ=π the centered derivative vanishes on the alternating grid mode; that is a resolution failure, not accurate transport. Underresolved wave packets can also have an incorrect group velocity.
The speed ratios assume a≠0. When a=0, this linearization has ωh=0 and the mode is stationary.
The sine relation is not a general nonlinear KEEP dispersion law. Finite-amplitude products couple modes and introduce aliasing questions. Kuya and Kawai’s 2022 split-form analysis treats that different problem: its nonlinear modified wavenumber cannot be replaced by this linearized example, and a finite-difference split form does not automatically remove aliasing. The authors also identify dispersion-error reduction as a reason for higher-order KEEP formulations (§2.4).
The figure compares the analytical spatial ratios for this uniform-state linear example. It is separate from the nonlinear saved vortex calculation below.
Spatial dispersion of the uniform-state linearization. Speed ratios approach one at low wavenumber; short waves have phase and group errors.

records.title: KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits
records.section: What changes when RK4 advances time?#

records.title: KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits
records.section: What changes when RK4 advances time?#
records.text:
\begin{aligned}\log|G|&=-\frac{\xi^6}{144}+O(\xi^8),\\\frac{\Omega\Delta t}{a k\Delta t}&=\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}\,\frac{-\arg_0R(-\mathrm i\xi)}{\xi}.\end{aligned}
For θ=π/2 and aΔt/h=0.5, the spatial phase-speed ratio is about 0.636620; including RK4 gives about 0.636317. The RK4 gain is about 0.999894878 per step and 0.989542 after 100 steps. These are calculations for one linear mode.
The small-ξ expansion shows phase lag near zero, but RK4 does not lag throughout its stable interval. At ξ=2, for example, its continuous phase is about 2.0344, ahead of the exact value 2.
The first factor in the last expression is spatial dispersion. The second is the additional RK4 phase error, with its limit taken at ξ=0. The accompanying response plot is for the scalar linear test equation; its amplitude is not a measured entropy error of the vortex.
There is no contradiction with conservation of the summed primary variables. If the discrete right-hand side has zero summed mass, momentum and total-energy residual at every stage, RK4 preserves those linear sums, apart from roundoff. K=m²/(2ρ), entropy, wave amplitudes and phases are nonlinear or more detailed properties; preserving the sums does not fix them. See the Runge–Kutta chapter for the stages and stability-function context.

records.title: KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits
records.section: Read the diagnostics separately#
records.text:
At fixed grid spacing, reduce Δt. Changes in amplitude and phase expose temporal error; the spatial dispersion remains.
Refine the grid as well, with sufficiently small temporal error. Refinement at fixed CFL changes both h and Δt, so it alone does not separate their contributions.
For small perturbations of a uniform state, compare one mode with its exact amplitude and phase. For a nonlinear vortex, compare fields and pressure-work/entropy diagnostics instead of applying the scalar sine relation to the whole flow.
Track primary conservation, kinetic-energy pressure-work balance, entropy-proxy change, density/pressure positivity, and field error separately. A dispersive oscillation is not automatically growing instability; conversely, actual growth cannot be dismissed as harmless dispersion.
The two response figures are analytical diagnostics, not additional atlas test problems. They do not change the published solver, fixed inputs, saved vortex results or code-edition ZIP. The existing vortex study below supplies the separate finite-grid evidence.

records.title: KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits
records.section: Appropriate first test: smooth isentropic vortex advection#
records.text:
Use gamma = 1.4 on a periodic [−10,10]² square, background velocity (1,0.5), and vortex strength beta = 3. Relative to its translating center, write X, Y and r² = X²+Y². The reference is
\begin{aligned}
u&=1-\frac{\beta Y}{2\pi}e^{(1-r^2)/2},&
v&=0.5+\frac{\beta X}{2\pi}e^{(1-r^2)/2},\\
T&=1-\frac{(\gamma-1)\beta^2}{8\gamma\pi^2}e^{1-r^2},&
\rho&=T^{1/(\gamma-1)},\qquad p=\rho^\gamma.
\end{aligned}
The whole-plane vortex translates analytically. Minimum-image coordinates in a box of length 20 leave its boundary tails below floating-point significance for these parameters, avoiding an appreciable periodic boundary jump. Positivity of the analytic temperature is checked explicitly.
The static study runs 48², 96², and 192² cells to t = 1 at CFL 0.25. It reports pointwise density L1 error, primary-conservation drift, and the change in S_* per mass. A separate 96² run halves the CFL to assess the time-step contribution. The measurement manifest states the actual errors; the expected smooth spatial order is two. The movie instead runs 96² to t = 4 and is a qualitative time-history exhibit, not a substitute for refinement.

records.title: KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits
records.section: Appropriate next tests#
records.text:
A compressible inviscid 3D Taylor–Green vortex is a primary KEEP benchmark. Fix the periodic box [0,2 pi]³, reference density, gamma, initial Mach number, velocity amplitude, initial pressure perturbation, and temporal scheme. Track total energy, kinetic energy, pressure dilatation, entropy, density/temperature RMS fluctuations, and resolved spectra under grid and time refinement. Pressure-work exchange must be separated from numerical dissipation. The original paper also examines inviscid isotropic turbulence. These 3D computations are not implemented in this edition; a 2D slice is not a replacement for the three-dimensional vortex-stretching dynamics.
A smooth constant-pressure density wave tests preservation of pressure/velocity equilibrium. It is a useful additional diagnostic, but that property depends on the flux variant. Our original arithmetic-mean flux produces a nonzero semidiscrete pressure residual for this data; a test records that limitation instead of claiming it passes. Shima et al. (2021) study pressure-equilibrium-preserving split forms.

records.title: KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits
records.section: Caveats: entropy, shocks, and the scheme version#
records.text:
Preserving is not a roundoff-exact entropy guarantee. The authors explicitly distinguish improved entropy behavior from exact conservation in their 2022 explanation. Tamaki, Kuya, and Kawai (2022) analyze remaining entropy errors and redefine KEEP variants with tunable approximation order. Our code does not implement that redefinition or an exact logarithmic-mean entropy-conservative flux.
A shock requires entropy production. A bare non-dissipative central flux supplies no general mechanism to select a non-oscillatory admissible shock solution. Sod, Shu–Osher, and Double Mach Reflection are not acceptance tests for the unstabilized baseline demonstrated here. A shock-tube run can still be a deliberate limitation/oscillation diagnostic; it should not be advertised as a validated shock-capturing result. It is inaccurate to turn this into a universal statement that every KEEP-based method is unable to solve any shock tube.
Shock stabilization changes the method. A sensor, artificial viscosity, upwind blending, filtering, or another entropy-stable construction needs its own definition and tests. Record shock/contact thickness, oscillations, positivity, and added dissipation; keep separate results for the smooth base scheme and stabilized extension. No such extension is implemented here.

records.title: KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits
records.section: Caveats: entropy, shocks, and the scheme version#
records.text:
No positivity theorem is supplied. Positive density and pressure in the displayed smooth runs do not establish robustness near vacuum or under arbitrary under-resolution. The code stops on nonphysical states rather than silently clipping them.
Time integration and boundaries matter. Asada, Maruyama, and Kawai (2024) address temporal preservation. Our RK4, periodic uniform-grid experiment does not implement their method, high-order/curvilinear KEEP, hanging-node treatments, wall models, or a production LES solver.

records.title: Lattice Boltzmann: collide, stream, recover fluid motion
records.section: Lattice Boltzmann: collide, stream, recover fluid motion
records.text:
Implemented: low-Mach, isothermal D2Q9–BGK, Guo body forcing, periodic
boundaries and stationary half-way bounce-back walls. Lattice units use
Δx=Δt=ρ_ref=1, c_s²=1/3.

records.title: Lattice Boltzmann: collide, stream, recover fluid motion
records.text:
The relaxation model of Bhatnagar–Gross–Krook (1954)
precedes lattice BGK. Qian–d'Humières–Lallemand (1992)
is the lattice-BGK reference. Guo–Zheng–Shi (2002)
supplies the force discretization used here. These are distinct developments.
D2Q9 has one resting population, four axial directions and four diagonals.
Weights are 4/9, 1/9 and 1/36 for those groups. The equilibrium is
f_q^{eq}=w_q\rho\left[1+3\boldsymbol c_q\cdot\boldsymbol u
+\frac92(\boldsymbol c_q\cdot\boldsymbol u)^2
-\frac32|\boldsymbol u|^2\right].
Collision relaxes populations, then streaming shifts each by its integer
lattice velocity:
f_q(\boldsymbol x+\boldsymbol c_q,t+1)
=f_q(\boldsymbol x,t)-\frac{f_q-f_q^{eq}}{\tau}+S_q.
For a force density F, Guo forcing uses
S_q=w_q\left(1-\frac1{2\tau}\right)
\left[3(\boldsymbol c_q-\boldsymbol u)
+9(\boldsymbol c_q\cdot\boldsymbol u)\boldsymbol c_q\right]\cdot\boldsymbol F,
\quad
\rho\boldsymbol u=\sum_q f_q\boldsymbol c_q+\frac{\boldsymbol F}{2}.
Density is the population sum, pressure is c_s²ρ, and viscosity is
ν=c_s²(τ−1/2). The Chapman–Enskog derivation
explains the discrete-time half-step correction. τ>1/2 makes this viscosity
positive; it is not a universal nonlinear stability certificate.

records.title: Lattice Boltzmann: collide, stream, recover fluid motion
records.section: Two independent tests#
records.text:
A transverse periodic shear wave decays as exp(−νk²t), allowing an independent
viscosity measurement. Force-driven Poiseuille flow has exact profile
u_x=F_x y(H−y)/(2ρ_refν). The walls sit half a lattice spacing beyond the
outer fluid nodes, not at those node centers. Fixed τ=0.8, peak velocity 0.01,
and Ny=8,16,32 test wall placement and refinement. Startup runs for twelve
slowest viscous decay times; finite-time and spatial errors remain distinct.
The data manifest records channel errors,
Mach numbers, force settings and step counts. Unit tests also verify periodic
mass/momentum conservation and equilibrium moments. BGK is a single-relaxation
baseline: MRT/TRT, entropic and cumulant collisions, thermal/compressible LBM,
moving walls and multiphase models remain extensions. Projection flow
solves a different discrete system and provides another route to incompressibility.

records.title: Level sets: moving interfaces and comparison with VOF
records.section: Level sets: moving interfaces and comparison with VOF
records.text: A level set embeds a curve or surface as the zero contour of a grid function and evolves that function. It connects transport, Hamilton–Jacobi equations and interface geometry, with a representation that naturally accommodates merging and splitting. Start with the equations, then inspect small reproducible two-dimensional circle motions.

records.title: Level sets: moving interfaces and comparison with VOF
records.section: Represent the interface by phi=0
records.text:
\Gamma(t)=\{\mathbf{x}:\phi(\mathbf{x},t)=0\},\qquad\phi<0\;\text{inside},\quad\phi>0\;\text{outside}
Here the interior is negative and the exterior positive. Function values are neither fluid density nor volume fraction. A monotone transformation retaining the zero set leaves the interface unchanged while changing gradients and numerical behavior. Some sources reverse the sign; normals and normal speeds must use the same convention.

records.title: Level sets: moving interfaces and comparison with VOF
records.section: An interface transported by a velocity
records.text:
\frac{D\phi}{Dt}=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\phi_t+\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla\phi=0
Differentiate the condition that phi is constant along a trajectory moving with velocity u to obtain the transport equation. Prescribed-velocity interface transport differs from solving coupled two-phase velocities and pressure. Upwind differences, ENO/WENO and time integration discretize this equation; they are choices in addition to the interface representation.

records.title: Level sets: moving interfaces and comparison with VOF
records.section: Normals, curvature and normal motion
records.text:
\phi_t+V_n\|
abla\phi\|=0,\qquad\mathbf{n}= rac{
abla\phi}{\|
abla\phi\|},\quad\kappa=
abla\cdot\mathbf{n}\phi(\mathbf{x})=\operatorname{sgn}(\phi)\operatorname{dist}(\mathbf{x},\Gamma),\qquad\|
abla\phi\|=1\quad	ext{where differentiable}
With a negative interior the normal points outward; the two-dimensional circle has kappa=1/r in this convention. A prescribed normal speed gives a Hamilton–Jacobi equation. A signed distance has unit gradient where differentiable; circle centers and points with nonunique nearest interfaces need not be smooth. Diagnostics therefore focus on a band near the interface; curvature-driven motion is explained but not executed here.

records.title: Level sets: moving interfaces and comparison with VOF
records.section: What redistancing repairs and can change
records.text:
\psi_\tau+S_\epsilon(\phi_0)(\|\nabla\psi\|-1)=0,\quad\psi(\mathbf{x},0)=\phi_0(\mathbf{x}),\quad S_\epsilon(z)=\frac{z}{\sqrt{z^2+\epsilon^2}}
General advection need not retain a distance function. An auxiliary pseudo-time tau equation can restore distance quality without advancing physical time t. Preserving an ideal zero set does not guarantee an interpolated discrete interface stays fixed. The example uses first-order Godunov iterations with sign frozen per call; it is not the constrained higher-order Sussman–Fatemi scheme, and no position or area improvement is assumed.

records.section: VOF: geometry and a volume balance
records.text: For a prescribed incompressible velocity, volume fractions admit conservative transport. Cancellation of shared interior face fluxes gives a global balance with boundary fluxes. Bounds0<=F<=1 additionally depend on fluxes, reconstruction and CFL conditions; conservation alone is insufficient. Conserving phi itself does not conserve its enclosed area. The area diagnosed from piecewise-linear phi here is not a conservatively advected VOF fraction.

records.section: Small 2D examples: translation and off-center rotation
records.text:
\phi_{\rm ref}(\mathbf{x},t)=\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}(t)\|-r,\quad \mathbf{c}_{\rm tr}(t)=\mathbf{c}_0+t\mathbf{v},\quad\mathbf{c}_{\rm rot}(t)=\mathbf{x}_c+R(\omega t)(\mathbf{c}_0-\mathbf{x}_c)
Radius.15 on the unit square, T=1. Translation starts at(.3,.35) with velocity(.2,.1). Rotation carries a circle centered at(.68,.5) once about(.5,.5), at angular speed2pi. records.title: Level sets: moving interfaces and comparison with VOF
records.section: What the error measurements mean
records.text:
E_\Gamma=\max_{t\in\{.25,.5,.75,1\}}\max_{\mathbf{z}\in Z_h(t)}\big|\|\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{c}(t)\|-r\big|,\quad p_{\rm obs}=\log_2\!\left(E_\Gamma(h)/E_\Gamma(h/2)\right)
Z_h contains linearly interpolated grid-edge zero crossings; E_Gamma is the maximum radial error at these samples, not a continuous-interface Hausdorff distance. Geometric area clips linear phi on triangles and compares against pi*r², retaining initial geometric bias. Coupled grid/time refinement of advection alone observes about1.90 for translation and2.02 for rotation. SeparateN64 CFL-halving sensitivity is recorded; this is not a proof of pure spatial order.
Finest-grid worst relative area error changes about0.22% to0.93% for translation and1.06% to2.02% for rotation, from advection alone to redistancing. The simple redistancing increases error in these fixed runs. Distance-gradient quality, zero-interface accuracy and enclosed-volume balance are distinct diagnostics.

records.title: Slope limiters: minmod, Superbee, MC, van Leer, and van Albada
records.section: Slope limiters: minmod, Superbee, MC, van Leer, and van Albada
records.text:
Limiters trade linear high-order reconstruction for a nonlinear choice of
local slope. Open the limiter notebook
to compare five choices on identical grids and time integrators, together with
first-order and unlimited scalar baselines.

records.title: Slope limiters: minmod, Superbee, MC, van Leer, and van Albada
records.section: Reconstruction and the ratio convention#
records.text:
For uniform cells, let the backward and forward increments be
a_i=\bar u_i-\bar u_{i-1},\qquad b_i=\bar u_{i+1}-\bar u_i,
\qquad r_i=a_i/b_i,\qquad s_i=\phi(r_i)b_i.
The two states reconstructed from cell i are
u_{i+1/2}^{L}=\bar u_i+\tfrac12s_i,\qquad
u_{i-1/2}^{R}=\bar u_i-\tfrac12s_i.
The implementation works directly with a and b, so a zero denominator at a
plateau requires neither a numerical epsilon nor an arbitrary ratio. Opposite
signs or either zero increment give zero limited slope. These are increments;
divide by cell width only if a derivative is required.

records.title: Slope limiters: minmod, Superbee, MC, van Leer, and van Albada
records.section: Five limiter functions#
records.text:
Each function below is zero for r ≤ 0. For r > 0:
\begin{aligned}
\phi_{\rm minmod}(r)&=\min(1,r),\\
\phi_{\rm Superbee}(r)&=\max\{\min(2r,1),\min(r,2)\},\\
\phi_{\rm MC}(r)&=\min\{2r,(1+r)/2,2\},\\
\phi_{\rm van\ Leer}(r)&=2r/(1+r),\\
\phi_{\rm van\ Albada}(r)&=(r^2+r)/(r^2+1).
\end{aligned}
This is the clipped, symmetric van Albada form, without an epsilon
regularization; other variants differ near extrema. MC means monotonized
central. All five satisfy phi(1)=1 and the plotted scalar bounds
0 ≤ phi(r) ≤ min(2r,2). See Sweby (1984)
for the scalar flux-limiter framework and Roe's compressive construction, and
the Clawpack limiter documentation
and MPI-AMRVAC slope-limiter notes
for implementation conventions. Names shared by different codes do not settle
which variables, time integrator, or epsilon are used.
Minmod chooses the smaller same-sign increment. Superbee takes a more
compressive slope and can sharpen a smooth feature into a plateau. MC and van
Leer retain more slope than minmod in many monotone regions. The notebook
lets the error, variation, and overshoot measurements qualify those tendencies;
no limiter wins every problem.

records.title: Slope limiters: minmod, Superbee, MC, van Leer, and van Albada
records.section: Computed comparisons#
records.text:
The scalar equation is u_t + a u_x = 0 on [0,1], with periodic boundaries.
All runs use conservative finite volumes, upwind interface fluxes, SSPRK(3,3),
N=200, |a| dt/dx ≤ 0.3, and final time 1. The last step is shortened. Both
directions a=±1 are computed. The two profiles are a unit square pulse on
[0.2,0.4] and sin(2πx). Initial and reference values are exact cell averages,
including partially covered square-pulse cells and the sine's sinc factor.
Displayed L1 errors use those cell averages. Periodic total variation includes
the last-to-first cell jump; mass is dx times the sum. Maximum TV uses every
saved full-step diagnostic, including the initial state.
The first-order comparison has zero slope. The unlimited comparison uses the
centered slope (a+b)/2 with the same flux and SSPRK3; it can produce oscillations.
It is not the Lax–Wendroff fully discrete method.
The separate Sod comparison uses the existing ideal-gas setup, gamma=1.4,
N=200, t=0.2, HLLC, primitive-variable reconstruction, and SSPRK3 at CFL=0.3.
Only the slope choice changes. Its density error is pointwise, following
the existing Sod convention; it is not an exact cell-average error. Outflow
boundaries mean that the periodic scalar mass/TV diagnostics are not applied
to this panel.
Smooth sine refinement at N=40,80,160 and t=0.2 reports measured L1 errors and

records.section: Computed comparisons#
records.text:
orders. A second-order label describes smooth-region consistency, not uniform
pointwise accuracy at extrema or a second-order error on discontinuities.

records.title: Slope limiters: minmod, Superbee, MC, van Leer, and van Albada
records.section: TVD is a property of the complete scalar update#
records.text:
For this scalar MUSCL operator, the stated slope bounds together with
|a| dt/dx ≤ 1/2 give a TVD forward-Euler building block; SSPRK3 preserves its
convex stability property under that bound. The executable solver restricts
CFL to this range. Tests check both signs, periodic conservation, full-step
variation, bounds, and a forward-Euler random-data case at CFL=1/2.
The same function applied componentwise to Euler primitive variables is not a
general system TVD theorem, entropy condition, or guarantee of positive cell
averages. Characteristic reconstruction and a fully discrete positivity
construction are separate extensions. See advanced limiters
for TVB extrema relaxation and conservative positive-state scaling.

records.title: Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes
records.section: Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes
records.text: Separate acoustic/convective preconditioning from transonic numerical-viscosity corrections. Connect a concrete Γ, a linear eigenvalue model, Mach cutoffs and dual time stepping with explicit variable conventions.

records.title: Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes
records.section: Matrix-solve and PDE preconditioning
records.text:
Left preconditioning P⁻¹Ax=P⁻¹b assists an iterative linear solve. Low-Mach PDE preconditioning instead changes pseudo-time mass matrices or characteristic numerical dissipation. Papers may use P for both; identify the operator being modified first.
At low Mach number, |u_n±a| is large compared with convection |u_n|, affecting steady iteration and low-speed flux accuracy. This is a different limit from a transonic characteristic u_n±a=0.

records.title: Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes
records.section: Place Γ on pseudo time
records.text:
Distinguish conservative U from primitive q and pseudo time τ from physical time t. Steady problems omit the physical-time term. Unsteady dual-time iterations retain the physically discretized term, such as BDF2, throughout the inner solve. Γ is not the same matrix as U_q.
For nonsingular Γ and unchanged R, a converged steady pseudo-time solve still satisfies R=0. Preconditioning spatial dissipation additionally changes the discrete residual construction. Indiscriminately preconditioning physical time changes the unsteady solution, including acoustics.
\Gamma(q)\frac{\partial q}{\partial\tau}+\frac{\partial U(q)}{\partial t}+R(U(q))=0,\qquad q=(p,u,v,w,T)^T.

records.title: Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes
records.section: A concrete Weiss–Smith-type matrix
records.text:
For a calorically perfect ideal gas, use q=(p,u,v,w,T), total specific enthalpy H=c_pT+(u²+v²+w²)/2, constant c_p, ρ_T=(∂ρ/∂T)_p and physical sound speed a. Θ replaces the usual pressure-density derivative. This ideal-gas specialization is not a general real-fluid formula.
Setting U_ref=a gives Θ=ρ/p and recovers the physical Jacobian U_q in this ordering. Reducing U_ref toward a convective scale changes pseudo-acoustic scales. Γ, its inverse and a conservative-variable P are not numerically identical matrices.
\Gamma=\begin{pmatrix}\Theta&0&0&0&\rho_T\\\Theta u&\rho&0&0&\rho_Tu\\\Theta v&0&\rho&0&\rho_Tv\\\Theta w&0&0&\rho&\rho_Tw\\\Theta H-1&\rho u&\rho v&\rho w&\rho_TH+\rho c_p\end{pmatrix},\qquad\Theta=\frac1{U_{\rm ref}^2}-\frac{\rho_T}{\rho c_p},\quad\rho_T=-\frac\rho T.

records.title: Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes
records.section: Stagnation singularities and a Mach cutoff
records.text:
A representative bounded parameter is shown below. Positive M_cut prevents U_ref=0 at stagnation; the upper bound recovers the physical system at supersonic speed. This is an illustrative choice, not a universal prescription: viscous, unsteady and boundary-aware variants use other reference scales.
The cutoff avoids degeneracy of the preconditioner near zero velocity; it does not remove physical Mach-1 flow from the domain. Too large a cutoff weakens low-Mach benefits; too small a value can impair robustness or boundary behavior.
M=\frac{\|\mathbf u\|}{a},\quad\beta=\min(1,\max(M,M_{\rm cut})),\quad U_{\rm ref}=\beta a,\quad 0<M_{\rm cut}\le1.

records.title: Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes
records.section: How characteristic eigenvalues change
records.text:
To expose the effect, linearize about constant density/sound speed and use pressure perturbation divided by ρ₀a, normal/tangential velocities and an advected entropy variable with fixed scaling. The following P is an illustrative pressure-row scaling, not the nonlinear Γ above.
For nonzero β comparable with Mach number, pseudo-acoustic eigenvalues become convective in scale. However, a matrix 2-norm condition number is a singular-value ratio, not generally an absolute-eigenvalue ratio. Examine normality, variable scaling, boundaries and discretization as well.
A=\begin{pmatrix}u_n&a&0&0\\a&u_n&0&0\\0&0&u_n&0\\0&0&0&u_n\end{pmatrix},\quad P=\operatorname{diag}(\beta^2,1,1,1),\quad q_\tau+PAq_x=0.\lambda_{\pm}=\frac{(1+\beta^2)u_n\pm\sqrt{(1-\beta^2)^2u_n^2+4\beta^2a^2}}2,\quad\lambda_0=u_n\ (\text{twice}),\quad\lambda_+\lambda_-=\beta^2(u_n^2-a^2).\kappa_2(A)=\sigma_{\max}(A)/\sigma_{\min}(A),\qquad\chi_\lambda(A)=\max_i|\lambda_i|/\min_{\lambda_i\ne0}|\lambda_i|.

records.title: Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes
records.section: Preconditioning does not remove a physical sonic zero
records.text:
The model has zero acoustic eigenvalue product when u_n²=a². More generally, multiplication by an invertible P cannot remove singularity of A. Do not claim that a preconditioning matrix eliminates physical sonic points. Sonic singularities of particular attempts at isotropic acoustic preconditioning also require formulation-specific discussion.
\det(PA)=\det(P)\det(A),\qquad P\text{ nonsingular}.

records.title: Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes
records.section: Transonic rarefaction and an entropy fix
records.text:
A Roe linearization can produce an unphysical expansion shock when a characteristic crosses zero through a rarefaction. A representative smoothing replaces |λ| in the numerical dissipation as below. δ has speed units; state-aware choices and fixed fractional cutoffs are different variants.
This modifies numerical viscosity rather than deleting the physical characteristic. The published acoustic quadratic smoothing is not claimed as a faithful reproduction of every Harten–Hyman construction. Entropy correction, HLLE low-density robustness, carbuncle control and low-Mach preconditioning address different problems.
\psi_\delta(\lambda)=\begin{cases}|\lambda|,&|\lambda|\ge\delta,\\(\lambda^2+\delta^2)/(2\delta),&|\lambda|<\delta,\end{cases}\qquad\delta>0.

records.title: Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes
records.section: Checks that keep the mechanisms separate
records.text:
Test spectra, recovery at β→1, low-Mach scaling and near-stagnation invertibility on small linear problems. Measure pseudo-time convergence separately from solution error due to changed spatial fluxes. Interior eigenvalue analysis alone cannot assess boundary reflection.
Use transonic Burgers/Euler rarefactions to examine expansion shocks, refinement and δ sensitivity. For unsteady problems separate physical-time convergence from inner pseudo-residual convergence. Low-Mach checks here are proposed work; existing Jacobi scaling or dual-time examples do not validate a dedicated low-Mach flow solver.

records.section: Publication scope and related entries
records.text:
Dedicated fixed-input code and verification cover Miczek-type spatial numerical-dissipation preconditioning in a 2D isentropic vortex. Ordinary and preconditioned Roe use unlimited primitive MUSCL, two background Mach values, three grids, 12 runs, T=.1 and SSPRK(3,3) with unchanged physical time and an acoustic CFL. See https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/validation/low-mach-vortex/?lang=en . Pseudo-time mass matrices Γ, the Weiss–Smith method, dual-time algorithms and steady-convergence acceleration remain reading-only. This spatial-dissipation example does not implement those algorithms or remove the physical acoustic time-step restriction. The original first-order pressure-gate failure and all earlier dated verification records are retained.

records.title: Markov-chain Monte Carlo / MCMC
records.section: Markov-chain Monte Carlo / MCMC
records.text: MCMC constructs a chain with a chosen invariant distribution. Invariance, finite-time mixing and accuracy for a particular observable are separate questions. Preserve the earlier unimodal Gaussian example while a separate scoped release examines multimodal mixing failures, diagnostic blind spots and independent implementation comparisons.

records.title: Markov-chain Monte Carlo / MCMC
records.section: Problem and representative equations
records.text:
For an unnormalized target π and proposal q(y|x), use the Metropolis–Hastings acceptance probability. Unknown target normalization cancels. Proposal factors cancel only for symmetric proposals; omitting them for an asymmetric proposal changes the target.
The new target is the one-dimensional equal-weight Gaussian mixture π(x)=[N(−6,1)+N(6,1)]/2. Compare moments, CDF and right-mode occupancy with known targets. It is one new test problem, distinct from the existing standard-normal target; different initializations, proposals and seeds do not add problems.
a(x,y)=\min\!\left(1,\frac{\pi(y)q(x\mid y)}{\pi(x)q(y\mid x)}\right),\qquad N_{\rm eff}\approx\frac{N}{1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_k}.

records.title: Markov-chain Monte Carlo / MCMC
records.section: Algorithm
records.text:
Propose y, accept or retain x, and keep rejected repetitions as samples. Assess initial transients and use dispersed initial states across chains. Interpret autocorrelation-based effective sample size only when stationarity and autocorrelation estimation are credible.
The new release distinguishes local random walks from dispersed mode-specific starts, local random walks with every chain starting in the same mode, and proposals containing reflection jumps that exploit the known symmetry x→−x. The last is a target-specific control, not a general solution for unknown multimodal distributions.
Evaluate x and the right-mode indicator separately. Preserve the old release’s classical split R-hat and mean-observable ESS; the new release adds rank-normalized split/folded R-hat and bulk/tail ESS as distinct definitions. ACF/ESS depend on the observable, sample budget, stationarity and estimator conventions; no single ESS universally characterizes a chain.
Do not use rank-transformed bulk ESS directly as an estimator of the raw-scale mean’s Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE). A library returning ESS=N for a constant observable is not evidence of good mixing.

records.title: Markov-chain Monte Carlo / MCMC
records.section: Conditions and pitfalls
records.text:
Detailed balance alone does not establish irreducibility or aperiodicity. Multimodality, correlations and boundaries can slow mixing. High acceptance can simply reflect tiny moves. Thinning is not a general way to increase information for a fixed computational budget.
Chains trapped in different modes can reveal a between-chain discrepancy, while chains all trapped in one mode can have R-hat near one despite a completely unexplored mode. Check known CDFs, mode occupancy and transitions alongside apparently favorable R-hat/ESS. Reflection-induced mode changes alone do not establish within-mode exploration.
Passing a test that intentionally reproduces poor mixing or a diagnostic blind spot does not mean estimation succeeded in that scenario. Fixed-input thresholds are acceptance criteria for this small comparison, not finite-run guarantees, diagnostic false-positive rates or reliability for every seed and target.
The local Gaussian random-walk MH used here is theoretically irreducible. Failure to leave a mode in a finite run is not described as a permanently nonergodic algorithm.

records.title: Markov-chain Monte Carlo / MCMC
records.section: What to check
records.text:
Check means, variances and quantiles for known targets, including asymmetric proposals and rejections. For multimodal cases report between-chain comparisons, autocorrelations, effective sample sizes and uncertainty; visually flat traces alone are not proof of convergence.
The new diagnostic controls compare ACF with direct summation on the same saved chains, and rank-normalized R-hat plus bulk/tail ESS with an independent ArviZ 0.20 execution. Keep IID, known-correlation and boundary controls such as constant series separate from estimation accuracy of the mixture sampler. Dedicated fixed inputs and references specify definitions, centering, splitting, ties, endpoints and the exact metrics compared.
For three scenarios and three fixed seeds, place distribution errors, mode occupancy/transitions and observable-specific diagnostics side by side. The old Gaussian release’s positive-sequence ESS and classical split R-hat remain unchanged and are not borrowed as verification of the new diagnostics.
Degenerate controls such as constant series and policies for nonfinite input are classification checks, separate from numerical agreement of finite diagnostics. The total number of reference-fixture fields is not presented as the number of numerical agreements.

records.title: Structured, unstructured, and triangular meshes
records.section: Structured, unstructured, and triangular meshes
records.text:
A mesh describes geometry and connectivity. Cell shape and indexing are different choices: triangles may be obtained by splitting a structured lattice, or connected in an irregular unstructured triangulation. The mesh explorer makes this distinction visible.
The element-basis chapter supplies the other half of the representation: Legendre modes, nodal Lagrange functions, quadrature and mass matrices, quadrilateral tensor products, and triangular P1/P2 shape functions. The basis notebook shows these functions inside a reference cell.

records.title: Structured, unstructured, and triangular meshes
records.section: Structured meshes#
records.text:
A logically rectangular mesh admits indices (i,j) and predictable neighboring indices. Cartesian rectangles are the simplest example, but a body-fitted curvilinear mesh may retain structured indexing. Metric terms, face normals, and cell volumes then come from its geometry. Multiblock grids join several such index spaces.
The explorer’s first example has 8 × 6 rectangular cells on the unit square. Connectivity is still exported explicitly so that the same inspection code can handle every example.

records.title: Structured, unstructured, and triangular meshes
records.section: Triangles and unstructured connectivity#
records.text:
Splitting each rectangle into two triangles changes the cell shape while preserving an underlying lattice pattern. The third example instead triangulates deterministic irregular interior points and a fixed square boundary. It uses Matplotlib’s Delaunay triangulation, not a call to the Triangle package. Shewchuk’s Triangle paper is a historical and algorithmic reading reference.
An unstructured solver normally stores vertices, cells, faces, and owner/neighbor relationships. Boundary faces have one adjacent cell; interior faces have two. The explorer highlights face-sharing neighbors, not every cell that merely touches a vertex. Labels are vertex-average cell centers; for triangles these equal the area centroids.

records.title: Structured, unstructured, and triangular meshes
records.section: Conservation is a face contract#
records.text:
For a finite volume K with area |K|,
\frac{d}{dt}(|K|\overline U_K)
=-\sum_{f\subset\partial K}|f|\,\widehat F(U_K,U_{K_f};n_{K,f}).
An interior face contributes equal and opposite fluxes to its two cells. This cancellation is independent of whether K is a quadrilateral or triangle. With counterclockwise vertices, an edge displacement (dx,dy) has outward unit normal (dy,−dx)/length. Signed polygon areas detect reversed or degenerate cells.

records.title: Structured, unstructured, and triangular meshes
records.section: Quality and implementation scope#
records.text:
Small angles, skewness, aspect ratio, nonorthogonality, and volume variation influence reconstruction and stability differently. Delaunay connectivity alone does not guarantee adequate boundary-layer resolution or a suitable minimum angle for arbitrary point sets. No mesh-quality optimization is performed here.
numart.geometry.example_meshes supplies the three examples. Tests verify positive cell areas, unit total area, connected face-neighbor graphs, reciprocal adjacency, and the planar Euler relation V−E+F_cells = 1 for these simply connected domains. The explorer is a geometry/connectivity demonstration; an unstructured Euler or viscous flow solver remains future work.
Continue with ALE moving cells, SPH particles, and cylindrical metrics and tensors.
