records.title: MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning
records.section: Problem and units#
records.text:
The original Orszag–Tang baseline is planar 2D ideal MHD with γ=5/3, μ0=1, and vz=Bz=0 on the
periodic unit square. Arrays are indexed [x,y,variable], with state
q=(ρ,mx,my,E,Bx,By,ψ) and
E=p/(γ-1)+ρ(vx²+vy²)/2+(Bx²+By²)/2.
The Orszag–Tang initial condition is
\rho=\frac{25}{36\pi},\quad p=\frac5{12\pi},\quad
\mathbf v=(-\sin2\pi y,\sin2\pi x),\quad
\mathbf B=\frac1{\sqrt{4\pi}}(-\sin2\pi y,\sin4\pi x).
This is a widely used compressible-test normalization, rather than a complete
reproduction of the original incompressible MHD study by
Orszag–Tang (1979).
The MASCLET paper is one reference for
this compressible normalization.

records.title: MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning
records.section: CT: share the same edge electric field#
records.text:
Store normal magnetic components on cell faces and update both directions
with a shared corner Ez: for example, Bx <- Bx - Δt D_y Ez and
By <- By + Δt D_x Ez. The corresponding divergence update contains
-D_xD_y Ez+D_yD_x Ez=0, preserving the matching discrete divergence.
This edition uses a simple flux-CT construction with arithmetic averages of
electric fields from Rusanov face fluxes. Face Riemann problems use a single
normal magnetic field; interface energy is adjusted to preserve primitive
pressure. After each update, cell-centered fields are averaged from faces.
Total energy is not reset nonconservatively. This implementation does not
reproduce every coordinate-system detail of Evans–Hawley or Athena's upwind CT.
Evans–Hawley (1988),
Tóth (2000).

records.title: MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning
records.section: GLM: transport and damp divergence errors#
records.text:
With cell-centered B and an auxiliary variable ψ, solve
\partial_t\mathbf B+\nabla\cdot(\mathbf v\mathbf B-\mathbf B\mathbf v)+\nabla\psi=0,
\qquad
\partial_t\psi+c_h^2\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=-\alpha\psi.
The induction flux components are F_i(B_j)=v_i B_j-B_i v_j+δij ψ.
This edition fixes ch=3 and uses α=damping*ch/h, with damping=0.18.
Linear ψ damping is split off and integrated exponentially; the remaining
update uses first-order Rusanov fluxes and forward Euler. The energy variable
is conventional MHD energy without a ψ² contribution. This educational
Dedner-type model covers a subset of GLM/EGLM formulations.
Dedner et al. (2002).

records.title: MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning
records.section: Measuring ∇·B#
records.text:
CT uses face-field differences; GLM uses centered differences of cell-centered
B. Records include the operator name, because values from different discrete
divergences cannot directly rank methods. With the fixed, relatively dissipative
GLM wave speed and symmetric OT data, centered divergence can remain extremely
small. OT alone therefore gives incomplete evidence about cleaning performance.
A separate diagnostic injects Bx += 0.01sin(2πx) with
magnetic_error=0.01, adjusting energy to preserve initial gas pressure.
This is not the standard OT problem. It examines divergence-wave transport
and damping while distinguishing damping from error reduction by numerical
viscosity. CT preserves an initial discrete constraint; it does not
automatically remove an existing magnetic-monopole error.

records.title: MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning
records.section: Verification scope#
records.text:
Tests check periodic mass and total energy, density and pressure positivity
on selected cases, CT divergence preservation, and GLM injected-error cleaning.
The HLLD section below adds Brio–Wu, Alfvén-wave refinement and field loops.
The initial teaching edition did not include external reference-code comparisons. The scoped additional releases are linked below. The low-resolution, first-order OT figures
are introductory demonstrations of magnetic-constraint handling.

records.title: MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning
records.section: Time evolution#
records.text: The motion gallery now includes separate 64² Orszag–Tang CT and GLM movies. Their actual adaptive-CFL snapshot times and native divergence diagnostics differ. Playback does not supply an equal-accuracy ranking.

records.title: MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning
records.section: HLLD and standard wave tests#
records.text:
Open the HLLD test comparisons. These new full-vector ideal-MHD
runs retain all three velocity and magnetic components, unlike the planar
Orszag–Tang baseline above. With μ0 = 1,
q = (ρ,ρvx,ρvy,ρvz,E,Bx,By,Bz) and
E = p/(γ−1) + ρ|v|²/2 + |B|²/2.
The HLLD fan resolves the contact and two rotational waves between its outer
fast-wave bounds. Intermediate star/double-star states use one shared normal
magnetic field. Invalid intermediate states fall back to HLLE and each face
fallback is counted. Miyoshi–Kusano (2005)
is the original bibliographic source; the accessible
Athena++ HLLD implementation
was used to cross-check the equations. This is an independent educational
implementation, not an Athena++ run or full reproduction of the paper.
All three tests use primitive MC slopes and SSPRK2 with face positivity
scaling. Step retries and HLLE fallbacks are recorded; no conserved mean is clipped.
Selected physical states staying positive is not a general robustness proof.
Brio–Wu: γ = 2 on [0,1], initial discontinuity at x = 0.5,
(ρ,p,By)L = (1,1,1), (ρ,p,By)R = (0.125,0.1,−1), Bx = 0.75,
all velocities and Bz zero, open ends, t = 0.1, CFL 0.35.
Compare HLLE/HLLD at 400 cells and HLLD at 800. Profiles are numerical
grid comparisons, not exact-solution overlays or a universal uniqueness
claim. Brio–Wu (1988).
Circular Alfvén wave: γ = 5/3, ρ = 1, p = 0.1, Bx = 1,

records.title: MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning
records.section: HLLD and standard wave tests#
records.text:
(By,Bz) = 0.1(cos(2πx),sin(2πx)), (vy,vz) = −(By,Bz), vx = 0,
periodic unit interval, one period t = 1, CFL 0.35. Exact conservative
cell averages include sinc-averaged transverse fields and constant total
energy; energy is not reconstructed from squares of averaged fields.
HLLE and HLLD use 32, 64, 128 and 256 cells. The finest measured orders
for the mean absolute transverse-field error are both approximately 1.98.
Weak magnetic loop: γ = 5/3, ρ = p = 1, v = (2,1,0),
Az = 10⁻³ max(0.3−r,0) on a periodic 2 × 1 box, t = 1,
CFL 0.3, 64 × 32 and 128 × 64 cells. Compare HLLE/HLLD with each
of CT and GLM. Finite-field translation is a diagnostic, not an exact
solution: magnetic forces are small, not zero.

records.title: MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning
records.section: CT-Contact and GLM scope in the loop test#
records.text:
CT initializes face B from a corner-potential curl. A contact-upwinded corner
EMF uses the face mass-flux sign for transverse electric-field derivatives
(CT-Contact in Mignone–Del Zanna (2021), equations 20–22).
It reduces to the face induction flux in a grid-aligned 1D limit. This is not
the UCT-HLLD construction. The shared curl preserves the native face divergence
at each SSPRK stage; cell B is averaged from faces and total energy is not reset.
GLM initializes cell B from a centered curl of cell Az. At each face, the
longitudinal subsystem is solved first:
 B_n^*=\frac{B_{n,L}+B_{n,R}}2-\frac{\psi_R-\psi_L}{2c_h},\qquad
 \psi^*=\frac{\psi_L+\psi_R}2-\frac{c_h(B_{n,R}-B_{n,L})}2.
HLLD/HLLE then receives common Bn*, preserving interface primitive pressure;
fluxes of Bn and ψ are ψ* and ch²Bn*. Set ch = 4 and use exponential ψ
half-step damping with rate 0.18ch/h before/after SSPRK2. E has no ψ energy.
This is a conservative GLM model inspired by the longitudinal solve in
Mignone–Tzeferacos (2010), not their CTU
integrator or EGLM variant. The fixed cleaning speed also changes the step count.
The initial magnetic discretizations and native divergence operators differ.
Energy fractions are normalized by each run's own initial cell-field energy.
Do not infer an equal-accuracy or matched-cost CT/GLM ranking. At 128 × 64,

records.title: MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning
records.section: CT-Contact and GLM scope in the loop test#
records.text:
CT preserves native maximum divergence below 4 × 10⁻¹⁶ in these runs;
GLM's centered maximum is about 3.7 × 10⁻⁴. These operator-dependent numbers
have units of B/length. All published loop runs have zero HLLE fallbacks and
zero retries. External-code validation of this earlier loop example, stronger-field loops
and UCT-HLLD remain unverified. Additional checks of other fixed problems
do not supply independent validation of this loop example.
Reproduce with python scripts/build_mhd_tests.py. Download
definitions, diagnostics and hashes and
computed conservative arrays.

records.title: MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning
records.section: Additional independent checks: matched conditions and separate errors
records.text:
These additional checks state their fixed inputs, independent references, and spatial and temporal refinement scope. Preserve the earlier teaching examples and their saved results without conflating discretizations or validation evidence.
The new comparisons use the same piecewise-constant reconstruction, LLF speed bound and actual forward-Euler step sequence, with GLM wave speed and physical damping rate fixed across grids. Discrete-system differences remain: face versus cell magnetic fields, CT shared electric fields and normal-field handling. The constructed exact solution is an educational advected magnetostatic equilibrium, not the existing standard Alfvén-wave test. A separate DOP853 integration of the same spatial RHS is distinguished from independent spatial-solver validation. Matching the LLF coefficient does not imply equal effective CT/GLM viscosity: CT corner averaging changes the discrete dissipation. Compare CT and GLM as whole discretizations; matched-viscosity damping controls apply only to the kappa=2/kappa=0 GLM companions.

records.title: MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning
records.section: Additional independent checks: matched conditions and separate errors
records.text: For the adopted constant-LLF-speed periodic discretization, commuting operators preserve the common centered zero divergence of the two physical cases. These cases check coupled-MHD accuracy and do not demonstrate active GLM damping. A separate constraint control supplies the same initial longitudinal divergence error. Preserving the initial face divergence is the expected CT result, while GLM wave transport and damping are checked against analytic references. An undamped companion and B²+psi²/ch² distinguish damping from wave phase and LLF numerical diffusion. This initially non-solenoidal control is not a physical solenoidal initial state or an additional physical problem. The earlier stand-alone GLM example’s phrase “a monopole mode that CT cannot represent” means it cannot arise from a CT initial state satisfying its divergence constraint; the new control deliberately violates that initial constraint.

records.title: MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning
records.section: Orszag–Tang: CT, GLM and independent Athena++
records.text:
Validation of a fixed physical problem
Compare CT and GLM density, magnetic field, conservation and div B for the same periodic Orszag–Tang data, against separately executed Athena++.
Face CT divergence and centered GLM divergence use different operators; common cell-centered diagnostics are also reported. Athena initializes face-averaged magnetic fields by differencing a vector potential, so comparison includes discretization differences of identical continuous data. This is a short planar test, not validation of shocks, 3D, UCT or CTU.

records.section: CT and GLM: mesh/time convergence of a moving magnetostatic equilibrium
records.text:
Validation of a fixed physical problem
Use a constructed exact equilibrium with nonzero magnetic force balanced by a pressure gradient, matching CT/GLM initial cell states, flux speed bound and time-step sequence.
With constant LLF viscosity and periodic centered operators, the GLM div=psi=0 subspace remains invariant up to roundoff. This tests coupled-MHD accuracy; a separate nonphysical control activates cleaning. p(q-average) is not the exact averaged p. DOP853 is independent in time only and shares the spatial RHS. records.title: MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning
records.section: Initial-constraint preservation by CT and active GLM cleaning: nonphysical control
records.text:
Diagnostic control; no additional physical problem
Intentionally begin with the same non-solenoidal cell B, checking that CT does not remove the initial defect and calibrating GLM’s B/psi response. This diagnostic adds no physical problem.
Passing means correctly detecting expected CT non-removal and the calibrated GLM response, not recommending non-solenoidal CT physical initial data. W is an auxiliary diagnostic norm, distinct from conserved physical total energy E without psi. B decay includes phase exchange and LLF diffusion; damping is assessed with the kappa0 control. No general nonlinear,boundary or shock cleaning guarantee is claimed.

records.title: Monte Carlo integration
records.section: Monte Carlo integration
records.text: Monte Carlo integration estimates an integral as an expectation. Accuracy depends on the sampling distribution, weights and variance, not merely on using random numbers.

records.title: Monte Carlo integration
records.section: Problem and representative equations
records.text:
Draw independent samples Xᵢ from a density p covering the support of f and average Yᵢ=f(Xᵢ)/p(Xᵢ). With finite second moment, estimate standard error by s_Y/√N. Uniform sampling requires the domain-volume factor.
I=\int f(x)\,dx=\mathbb E_p\!\left[\frac{f(X)}{p(X)}\right],\qquad \widehat I_N=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{f(X_i)}{p(X_i)},\quad\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}=s_Y/\sqrt N.

records.title: Monte Carlo integration
records.section: Algorithm
records.text: Specify the distribution and random generator, draw samples and compute the weighted mean and variance. Importance sampling concentrates p where contributions matter, while monitoring heavy tails of f/p. Record generator/version, seed and sample count for reproducibility.

records.title: Monte Carlo integration
records.section: Conditions and pitfalls
records.text: The N⁻¹/² scale is statistical and conditional on assumptions such as independence and finite variance; it is not a deterministic bound for each run. Rare events and missed peaks can make variance estimates misleading. Correlated MCMC samples need a different uncertainty calculation.

records.title: Monte Carlo integration
records.section: What to check
records.text: Use repeated independent runs on known integrals to examine N scaling and interval coverage. Record actual mean error separately from estimated uncertainty, and verify that changes in importance density preserve the target integral.

records.title: Monte Carlo integration
records.section: Publication scope and related entries
records.text:
Integrate x² under U[0,1]. Compare 256 independent seeds with analytic integral and variance, checking N^-1/2 RMS scaling and interval coverage. Excludes MCMC and rare events. Inputs, code, measured values and tolerances are linked from the method and execution pages. Not every general verification proposal above has been executed.

records.title: Time-dependent tests: movies and saved states
records.section: Time-dependent tests: movies and saved states
records.text:
Open the motion gallery.
Use movies when the evolution is part of the question: a shock reflecting, a vortex advecting, or magnetic structures forming. Steady solutions, manufactured equilibrium profiles, and final elliptic fields remain still figures. A solver residual versus iteration is an algorithmic history, not a physical-time flow movie.

records.title: Time-dependent tests: movies and saved states
records.section: Five computed movies#
records.text:
Double Mach Reflection: Mach-10 2D Euler reflection on 256 × 64 cells, t = 0 to 0.2, first-order HLL with SSPRK2 and CFL 0.4. The fine wall jet is not resolved. Read the setup.
Orszag–Tang with CT: 64² periodic planar ideal MHD, t = 0 to 0.5, first-order Rusanov with forward Euler and CFL 0.3. Magnetic divergence uses the staggered face operator.
Orszag–Tang with GLM: the same resolution and physical interval, with fixed cleaning speed 3 and damping 0.18. Its native divergence uses the cell-centered central operator. The CT and GLM plots do not form an equal-accuracy ranking. Read the MHD definitions.
Smooth isentropic vortex with original KEEP: 96² periodic Euler on [−10,10]², t = 0 to 4, the second-order arithmetic-mean Cartesian KEEP flux and classical RK4, CFL 0.25. No shock stabilization, pressure-equilibrium-preserving extension, or exact entropy claim is included. Read the KEEP chapter.
Mach-3 forward-facing step: 240 × 80 cells, t = 0 to 4, first-order HLL and SSPRK2 with CFL 0.4. Grid-aligned blocked cells represent a step at x = 0.6 of height 0.2. Standard reflection is applied without an entropy/enthalpy corner reset. Diagnostics exclude solid cells. This is a classical inviscid benchmark, not a NASA experimental validation. See the shock-case definitions.

records.title: Time-dependent tests: movies and saved states
records.section: Five computed movies#
records.text: Density and pressure appear together in every movie. These are rendered numerical states from the repository solvers, not interpolated illustrations or reproductions of original-paper movies.

records.title: Time-dependent tests: movies and saved states
records.section: Actual physical times, unchanged time steps#
records.text:
Each movie requests 81 output times, including the initial and final times. The recorder saves the first completed solver state at or after each request. It does not shorten a numerical step to hit a requested time and does not interpolate the solution. If a coarse step crosses several requests, one state represents them. Actual times and solver step counts accompany every frame.
The production movies have 81 distinct states each. The MHD CT and GLM solvers choose different time steps, so similarly numbered frames need not have identical intermediate physical times. Read the timestamps before comparing them. Snapshot tests verify that enabling output leaves the final state and numerical history unchanged.

records.title: Time-dependent tests: movies and saved states
records.section: Fixed scales and explicit playback#
records.text:
Each density and pressure color scale is fixed across its entire run using that run’s extrema over the saved states. Colors must not be interpreted as identical values across different movies unless their scale labels agree. The minima and maxima listed beside the player are measurements of the currently displayed state; they do not establish a positivity theorem.
Playback starts only after pressing Play. Pause, first/last, previous/next, a saved-frame slider, speed selection, and an optional loop support inspection. Speed is presentation speed, not a change to the simulation. At the nominal rate, 81 saved frames at 12 frames per second make a 6.75-second clip. All physical times remain printed inside the images.
A native MP4 player and MP4/frame downloads are also available. MP4 uses H.264 video with no audio; the inspectable image frames are lossless WebP. Video compression is a presentation step and never feeds back into the computation.

records.title: Time-dependent tests: movies and saved states
records.section: Reproduce and verify#
records.text:
python -m pip install '.[movies]'
python scripts/build_movies.py
python scripts/check_movies.py
The builder writes the published frames, MP4 files, and movie catalog into website/public/assets/movies. It also saves full numerical snapshots as compressed NumPy arrays in the ignored outputs/movies directory for local inspection. Source hashes, image/video hashes, numerical-state hashes, software versions, methods, boundary conditions, physical scales, and per-frame diagnostics are recorded in the catalog. The fifth movie is built by python scripts/build_shock_gallery.py and has a separate shock catalog; the player combines both catalogs. Its full saved states are in outputs/shock-gallery.
The checker validates hashes and metadata, opens each saved image, and decodes each MP4 to verify its dimensions, playback rate, and complete frame count. A short small-grid build can be made with --quick --output <directory>; its catalog is marked as a quick check and is not the published production run.

records.section: What a movie does not establish#
records.text: A visually smooth evolution does not establish mesh convergence, an entropy inequality, shock robustness, long-time turbulent accuracy, or agreement with experiments. The KEEP vortex refinement supplies separate smooth-error measurements. The carbuncle chapter explains why a shock movie alone cannot certify multidimensional stability.

records.title: NASA 2D verification and validation case catalog
records.section: Computed shock tests#
records.text:
Open the shock-containing fields in the gallery.
Both wedges start from uniform freestream with gamma 1.4, density 1 and sound
speed 1. The independent body-fitted mesh spans x = −0.5 to 1, the lower wall
y = max(x,0) tan(15°), and the upper boundary y = 1.2. The higher farfield keeps
the Mach-2 weak shock below that boundary at the outlet; it differs from the
height 1 of NASA's Mach-2.5 domain. Inlet and upper-boundary
states are fixed at freestream, the outlet is extrapolated and the lower wall
reflects normal momentum. Shared oriented face fluxes conserve the cell totals;
cell areas and face normals come from the actual quadrilaterals.
NASA wedge, Mach 2.0: Mach and pressure maps on 240 × 80 cells at t = 3,
with the theoretical weak-shock line. A 120 × 40 run supplies a second grid.
NASA setup.
NASA wedge, Mach 2.5: the same independent meshes and terminal time.
The reference shock angle is approximately 36.94490°, pressure ratio 2.467500,
and downstream Mach number 1.873526. The theta–beta–Mach root and normal-shock
relations supply the reference, with a numerical Rankine–Hugoniot check.
NASA analytical comparison.
Classical Mach-3 forward-facing step: a 3 × 1 tunnel with the step at
x = 0.6 and height 0.2, uniform inflow (density 1.4, pressure 1, velocity 3),
reflecting walls and an extrapolated exit. A 240 × 80 grid reaches t = 4,

records.title: NASA 2D verification and validation case catalog
records.section: Computed shock tests#
records.text:
with 81 saved states and an MP4. Watch the shock reflections.
This is the classical Emery/Woodward–Colella benchmark, not a NASA-originated
experiment. The corner treatment differs from the corrected PPM comparison
in Woodward–Colella §VI.b:
this baseline applies plain reflection and does not reset entropy or enthalpy
near the step corner. Corner artifacts and smeared slip lines may remain.
These use first-order HLL finite volumes and SSPRK2, with CFL 0.4. Wedges
have no imposed analytical shock in their initial state. Their normalized L1
density errors compare conservative cell averages with an exactly clipped
piecewise-constant oblique-shock reference. Wall-pressure medians use the first
fluid row over 0.5 < x < 0.9; a density-gradient fit over 0.35 < x < 0.85 estimates
the shock angle. Mach-2 MC still has local time variation at t = 3 (maximum conserved update
rate approximately 6.08 in the published run); it is not a converged steady
solution. This residual is exposed alongside the sharper density error.
Two grids at one finite terminal time do not establish general
asymptotic order or complete steady convergence. The step has no exact overlay
and only one published grid; t = 4 is an unsteady snapshot.

records.title: Operator splitting: Lie–Trotter and Strang
records.section: Operator splitting: Lie–Trotter and Strang
records.text: Operator splitting advances separate parts of an evolution equation and composes their solution maps. Lie–Trotter uses two full substeps; Strang surrounds one full substep with two half substeps. Even exact subproblem solutions leave a composition error when their order matters.

records.title: Operator splitting: Lie–Trotter and Strang
records.section: Split the evolution, define one time step
records.text:
\dot u=F(u)+G(u),\qquad \dot v=F(v)\ \Rightarrow\ \varphi_F^h,\qquad \dot w=G(w)\ \Rightarrow\ \varphi_G^h.
Start with a sufficiently smooth autonomous finite-dimensional initial-value problem. Each φ is the exact flow of its subproblem, and h is one step for the summed equation. Compositions act from right to left. Advancing F for h and then G for h approximates one step of length h for the original equation, not 2h. Using only h/2 for each part would instead halve the leading vector field.
The approach uses tractable subproblems such as reaction and diffusion, transport and sources, or drift and force in a separable Hamiltonian. Splitting is a separate choice from spatial discretization and physical modeling. Matrix exponentials below apply to the linear specialization F(u)=Au, G(u)=Bu.

records.title: Operator splitting: Lie–Trotter and Strang
records.section: Lie–Trotter: two ordered full substeps
records.text:
u^{n+1}=L_h(u^n)=(\varphi_G^h\circ\varphi_F^h)(u^n),\qquad L_h=e^{hB}e^{hA}\quad(\dot u=(A+B)u).
Our convention applies F first and G to the updated state. Reversing the order gives another first-order method, generally with a different value. Computing both substeps independently from the old state and adding their increments is a different update.
e^{hB}e^{hA}-e^{h(A+B)}=\frac{h^2}{2}(BA-AB)+O(h^3),\qquad [A,B]=AB-BA.
Expand both exponentials through h²: the commutator remains in the difference from the exact summed flow. Its sign here follows the chosen product and reverses with the substep order. The local defect means the one-step difference starting from an exact state: O(h²). Under stability and smoothness, accumulated error at a fixed final time is O(h). The product limit and a finite-step error estimate are separate statements.

records.title: Operator splitting: Lie–Trotter and Strang
records.section: Strang: a symmetric second-order composition
records.text:
u^{n+1}=S_h(u^n)=(\varphi_F^{h/2}\circ\varphi_G^h\circ\varphi_F^{h/2})(u^n),\qquad S_h=e^{hA/2}e^{hB}e^{hA/2}.
Apply a half F step, a full G step and another half F step, each to the current state. G/2→F→G/2 is another valid Strang variant. The two variants generally produce different numerical solutions and error constants.
S_{-h}=S_h^{-1},\qquad S_h-e^{h(A+B)}=O(h^3),\qquad [A,B]=0\ \Rightarrow\ L_h=S_h=e^{h(A+B)}.
When inverse flows exist, replacing h by −h reverses the symmetric composition. Expansion through the quadratic term cancels the leading Lie–Trotter defect, leaving local O(h³) and global O(h²) errors; nested commutators enter the next error terms. For commuting finite matrices, both exact-subflow compositions equal the exact summed flow. Extending this statement to unbounded PDE operators requires domain and regularity conditions.

records.title: Operator splitting: Lie–Trotter and Strang
records.section: Compare order, symmetry and work
records.text:
Smooth, stable finite-time problems with exact subflows
PropertyLie–TrotterStrang
Application orderF(h), G(h)F(h/2), G(h), F(h/2)
One-step local defectO(h²)O(h³)
Global error at fixed final timeO(h)O(h²)
Time symmetry with exact subflowsGenerally absentYes, for invertible flows
Subflow calls per standalone step23
Asymptotic error reduction on halving hAbout 2About 4
E(h)=\|u_N-u(T)\|_2,\quad h=T/N,\qquad p_{\rm obs}=\log_2\frac{E(h)}{E(h/2)},\qquad E_L(h)=O(h),\ E_S(h)=O(h^2).
A standalone Strang step calls one additional subflow. Over consecutive constant steps, adjacent half F steps can be merged when the exact flow has the group property (a positive-time semigroup suffices for diffusion). Lie–Trotter uses 2N subflow calls and merged Strang 2N+1. Actual work depends on each subproblem, output and boundary processing, and whether numerical subflows permit merging. Call counts are not measured runtimes.

records.title: Operator splitting: Lie–Trotter and Strang
records.section: Small noncommuting example with exact subflows
records.text:
u=\begin{pmatrix}q\\p\end{pmatrix},\quad A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad B=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad u(0)=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},\quad u(t)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t\\-\sin t\end{pmatrix}.
\varphi_A^h(q,p)=(q+hp,p),\qquad\varphi_B^h(q,p)=(q,p-hq),\qquad [A,B]=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
L_hu_0=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-h\end{pmatrix},\quad S_hu_0=\begin{pmatrix}1-h^2/2\\-h\end{pmatrix},\quad u(h)=\begin{pmatrix}1-h^2/2+O(h^4)\\-h+h^3/6+O(h^5)\end{pmatrix}.
This is a two-component harmonic oscillator with nondimensional q, p and time. Its subflows require only addition and multiplication; the reference is the analytic sine/cosine solution. The first-step formulas already expose the local defect orders. Use the norm of both components to avoid mistaking componentwise cancellation for higher order. This lightweight illustration uses no spatial grid, independent PDE implementation or quantum-chemistry calculation.

records.title: Operator splitting: Lie–Trotter and Strang
records.section: Small noncommuting example with exact subflows
records.text: These saved values were recomputed for the fixed input u₀=(1,0), T=1 and N=8,16,32,64. The final global observed orders are 0.9983 for Lie–Trotter and 2.0002 for Strang. A separate single-step check from the exact initial state gives local orders near 2 and 3. Controls check that reversed Lie–Trotter remains first order with a different solution, and that commuting A=−I, B=−2I agrees with exp(−3T) to floating-point roundoff.

records.title: Operator splitting: Lie–Trotter and Strang
records.section: Conditions: order and stability can be lost
records.text:
The stated orders assume a smooth solution, sufficiently small steps, a fixed finite interval and suitable stability. Shocks, stiff relaxation and nonsmooth initial data can invalidate those expectations. PDE subproblems and their stages need compatible boundary data. Check order reduction from inhomogeneous or time-dependent boundaries separately from spatial and nonlinear-solver errors.
A symmetric arrangement alone does not make approximate subflows second order. Standard Strang composition needs subsolvers with at least second-order consistency and sufficiently tight iteration tolerances to retain second order. Exact or symmetric subsolvers are needed to retain time symmetry as well. Direct substitution of forward or backward Euler generally reduces the order to one. Nonautonomous problems require a suitable extended system including time, or consistent subproblem time arguments; freezing everything at the old time is not enough.
\det L_h=\det S_h=1,\quad\operatorname{tr}L_h=\operatorname{tr}S_h=2-h^2,\quad 0<|h|<2\quad\text{(oscillator)}.

records.title: Operator splitting: Lie–Trotter and Strang
records.section: Conditions: order and stability can be lost
records.text: For this oscillator both update matrices have determinant 1 and trace 2−h², giving bounded oscillatory modes for 0<|h|<2. Exact subflows do not by themselves guarantee unconditional stability. Composition inherits only properties preserved by its submaps: Hamiltonian symplecticity does not imply positivity for arbitrary reactions or exact conservation of the full energy.

records.title: Operator splitting: Lie–Trotter and Strang
records.section: Existing Strang examples and the distinction from IMEX
records.text:
The existing reaction–diffusion finite-amplitude Schnakenberg and saturated-pattern examples use exact half steps of centered-difference diffusion and a full implicit-midpoint reaction step in a Strang composition. Their published records give spatial and temporal checks for those fixed conditions. They are separate from this oscillator illustration, and their distributions, tolerances and results are preserved.
IMEX also separates parts of the right-hand side, but IMEX time integration combines explicit and implicit stage equations, whereas the splitting here composes subproblem flows. These are different updates. For the separable-Hamiltonian connection, see symplectic integration.

records.title: Gradient and quasi-Newton optimization
records.section: Gradient and quasi-Newton optimization
records.text: Gradient methods use first derivatives; quasi-Newton methods infer curvature from gradient differences. This introduction treats smooth unconstrained minimization, separately from constrained optimality conditions.

records.title: Gradient and quasi-Newton optimization
records.section: Problem and representative equations
records.text:
Let gₖ=∇f(xₖ), Hₖ approximate the inverse Hessian and pₖ=−Hₖgₖ. In BFGS, s=xₖ₊₁−xₖ, y=gₖ₊₁−gₖ and ρ=1/(yᵀs). Hₖ=I gives steepest descent in the chosen coordinates, so units and scaling matter.
x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kH_kg_k,\qquad H_{k+1}=(I-\rho sy^T)H_k(I-\rho ys^T)+\rho ss^T.

records.title: Gradient and quasi-Newton optimization
records.section: Algorithm
records.text: Evaluate gradients, select a step length using a line search and update curvature. BFGS enforces Hₖ₊₁y=s with a symmetric update. Positive-definite Hₖ and yᵀs>0 preserve positive definiteness. Poor curvature requires an explicit policy such as skipping or damping the update.

records.title: Gradient and quasi-Newton optimization
records.section: Conditions and pitfalls
records.text: For nonconvex problems, finding a local stationary point is different from finding a global optimum. Noisy gradients, nonsmooth objectives and inaccurate inner PDE solves can corrupt curvature. Do not stop on relative objective change alone: inspect gradient norms, step sizes, limits and termination reasons.

records.title: Gradient and quasi-Newton optimization
records.section: What to check
records.text:
Vary conditioning on positive-definite quadratics with known minima and check gradients by directional differences. On curved valleys vary initialization, scaling and line searches. Decreasing an objective does not validate physical assumptions or constraints.

records.title: Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid
records.section: Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid
records.text: Poisson solvers and particle force algorithms answer related questions with different representations. Begin by fixing the Green function, boundary conditions, mass assignment, softening, and force operator. A periodic PM field and an isolated direct-sum field solve different problems, so their raw difference is not a force-accuracy measurement.

records.title: Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid
records.section: Particle–mesh: mass to potential to force#
records.text:
In a three-dimensional periodic cube,
\nabla^2\phi=4\pi G(\rho-\overline\rho),\qquad
\widehat\phi(\boldsymbol k)=-\frac{4\pi G}{|\boldsymbol k|^2}\widehat\rho(\boldsymbol k)
\quad(\boldsymbol k\ne0),\qquad \widehat\phi(0)=0.
Subtracting the mean supplies the periodic compatibility condition; setting the potential’s zero mode fixes its gauge. This choice differs from an isolated sheet, whose horizontal mean produces a real vertical force.
PM deposits particle masses onto a grid, solves the mesh Poisson equation, differentiates the potential, and interpolates acceleration back to particles. The example uses cloud-in-cell (CIC) weights on eight neighboring mesh nodes in 3D, a continuum Fourier Laplacian symbol, and spectral force derivatives. An even-grid derivative sets its unpaired Nyquist mode to zero. Matched CIC deposition/interpolation and an odd force operator yield zero total internal force to roundoff in the tested periodic example.
Assignment and interpolation smooth the force. The mesh Green function, discrete derivative, aliasing, grid anisotropy, and any deconvolution all influence the effective particle interaction. Accurate solution of a manufactured mesh mode does not establish accurate close-pair forces.

records.title: Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid
records.section: P³M: correct the near field without counting it twice#

records.title: Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid
records.section: Barnes–Hut Tree: open the nearby cells#
records.text:
Barnes and Hut (1986) organize particles into an octree. A distant cell is approximated by its mass distribution moments; nearby cells are opened recursively. Our geometric acceptance test is s/d < theta, with cell side s and distance d to its center of mass. A node containing the target is always opened, and direct leaves exclude self-interaction.
The implemented isolated reference uses G = 1 and Plummer softening:
\boldsymbol a_i=-\sum_{j\ne i}m_j
\frac{\boldsymbol x_i-\boldsymbol x_j}
{(|\boldsymbol x_i-\boldsymbol x_j|^2+\epsilon^2)^{3/2}}.
The Tree and direct sum use identical particles, masses, and epsilon. Smaller theta usually trades more interactions for lower error, but individual-particle errors need not decrease monotonically. The familiar O(N log N) description is a typical algorithmic scaling under suitable distributions, not a timing result or worst-case guarantee for this Python example.

records.title: Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid
records.section: Multipole expansion: monopole and second moments#
records.text:
Let R point from a cell’s center of mass to the target, delta_a be source offsets, M be total mass, and S = sum m_a delta_a delta_a^T. The center-of-mass dipole vanishes. With s² = R²+epsilon², a Taylor expansion of the same softened kernel gives
\phi(\boldsymbol R)\approx-G\left[
\frac{M}{s}+\frac{3\boldsymbol R^T S\boldsymbol R}{2s^5}
-\frac{\operatorname{tr}S}{2s^3}\right].
The code differentiates this potential analytically. It retains the full second moment, including its trace; silently substituting an unsoftened traceless quadrupole formula would change the approximation. The gallery compares monopole and second-moment errors against the same direct force sum.
A fast multipole method also forms and translates local expansions, reusing cell-to-cell interactions. It is more than adding a quadrupole to Barnes–Hut. Greengard and Rokhlin (1987) are the original FMM reading reference; FMM translations are not implemented here.

records.title: Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid
records.section: TreePM: a different near-field evaluator#
records.text:
TreePM combines a mesh long-range field with a short-range Tree field. A representative Gaussian potential split has
\widehat\phi_{\rm long}=\widehat\phi\,e^{-k^2r_s^2},\qquad
\phi_{\rm short}(r)=-\frac{Gm}{r}\operatorname{erfc}\left(\frac{r}{2r_s}\right).
The short-range force is the derivative of this potential, not merely Newton’s force times erfc. Cutoffs, periodicity, and softening must match the split. Springel’s GADGET-2 paper provides a primary example. The two independent PM and Tree examples here do not constitute an implemented TreePM solver.

records.title: Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid
records.section: Where multigrid belongs#
records.text:
Multigrid solves a discretized elliptic equation rather than directly summing particle pairs. A smoother reduces oscillatory error; restriction, a coarse solve, prolongation, and correction address smoother error components. It can replace the grid Poisson solve inside a particle–mesh pipeline, provided its operator, boundary treatment, and particle coupling are specified.
The existing multigrid implementation solves a 2D five-point negative-Laplacian problem with zero Dirichlet boundaries. It is not yet the isolated 3D particle-gravity solver. Boundary values for an isolated finite mesh may be supplied by multipoles or another open-boundary construction; setting phi = 0 at a nearby box face generally does not reproduce phi tending to zero at infinity.

records.title: Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid
records.section: Reproduce the static checks#
records.text:
python scripts/build_particle_gravity.py
This creates the figure and measurement manifest. The Tree experiment uses 192 equal-mass particles, seed 17, epsilon = 0.03, five opening angles, and both moment orders. Its error is ||a_tree−a_direct||₂ / ||a_direct||₂. Counts of accepted nodes and direct pairs are reported; their operation costs differ, so their sum is not a timing comparison.
The PM test uses a 24³ periodic mesh. A separate density 1+0.2 cos(2 pi x) has potential −0.2 cos(2 pi x)/pi for G = 1. Tests cover CIC mass conservation, periodic wrapping, constant interpolation, self-force, net force, the manufactured Poisson mode, exact Tree opening at theta = 0, and selected force-error refinements. A target-by-target approximate Tree need not preserve pairwise momentum exactly; the manifest records a net-force diagnostic.
Continue with isolated FFT and slab Green functions, and the symplectic map chapter for the additional requirements on force consistency and time integration.

records.title: Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid
records.section: A separate model: 2D logarithmic FMM
records.text:
The gravity, PM and tree article and its boundary conventions above are preserved. The following FMM is a separate educational model: a negative-logarithmic kernel in 2D free space evaluated with a uniform quadtree. Its accuracy does not transfer to 3D Coulomb or softened-gravity 1/r kernels.

records.title: Particle methods and smoothed particle hydrodynamics
records.section: Particle methods and smoothed particle hydrodynamics
records.text: Lagrangian particles carry quantities while moving with a flow. SPH replaces a field value or derivative by a local kernel-weighted particle sum. The independent early papers by Gingold and Monaghan (1977) and Lucy (1977) are historical starting points. The static reconstruction below does not reproduce their stellar calculations.

records.title: Particle methods and smoothed particle hydrodynamics
records.section: From an integral to particles#
records.text:
A smoothed field is approximated by
f_h(x)=\int f(x')W(x-x',h)\,dx'
\approx\sum_b \frac{m_b}{\rho_b} f_b W(x-x_b,h).
The volume weight m_b/rho_b matters. Smoothing length h is a kernel scale, not necessarily the particle spacing. Compact support defines the neighbor search; it does not impose a fixed mesh connectivity.
Our one-dimensional example uses the normalized cubic spline, with q = |x|/h:
W(x,h)=\frac{2}{3h}\begin{cases}
1-\frac32q^2+\frac34q^3,&0\le q<1,\\
\frac14(2-q)^3,&1\le q<2,\\
0,&q\ge2.
\end{cases}
This prefactor is one-dimensional. Two- and three-dimensional kernels require different normalization constants.

records.title: Particle methods and smoothed particle hydrodynamics
records.section: Partition of unity and correction#
records.text:
The raw sum of particle volumes times W need not equal one on a discrete particle set. A Shepard-normalized interpolant divides by that sum. It reproduces a constant wherever the denominator is nonzero, but this interpolation correction alone does not establish conservative dynamics, linear consistency, or stable pressure forces.
import numpy as np
from numart.geometry import sph_reconstruct
p = (np.arange(64) + 0.5) / 64
x = np.linspace(0, 1, 201)
f, partition = sph_reconstruct(x, p, np.sin(2*np.pi*p), h=0.04)
f_corrected, _ = sph_reconstruct(x, p, np.sin(2*np.pi*p), h=0.04, normalize=True)
The routine uses periodic minimum-image distances on [0,1] and equal volume weights 1/N. It requires 0 < h < 1/4 so the support fits the minimum-image convention. It does not infer physical density from arbitrary unequal particle spacings.

records.title: Particle methods and smoothed particle hydrodynamics
records.section: What a fluid solver would additionally need#
records.text:
Density estimation or a continuity update, a consistent pressure force, momentum and energy evolution, boundary particles, time stepping, neighbor-search updates, and treatment of shocks or tensile/pairing instabilities are additional modeling decisions. Artificial viscosity used in shock-capturing SPH must be distinguished from the physical Newtonian viscous stress tensor.
Tests check the continuous kernel’s normalization and discrete constant reproduction after normalization. This edition implements kernel reconstruction only, not an SPH flow solver. See time integration for why a particle kick–drift leapfrog and a two-step first-order ODE leapfrog should not be conflated.

records.title: Particle methods and smoothed particle hydrodynamics
records.section: Particle gravity is a separate operator#
records.text: PM, P³M, Tree, and multipole methods compute gravitational fields; SPH kernels reconstruct fluid quantities and their derivatives. Read particle gravity, isolated and slab boundary kernels, and symplectic time integration to connect these different parts of a self-gravitating particle model.

records.title: Periodic DFT: Γ points, k-point integration, basis sets, SCF and an independent reference
records.section: The fixed physical model and the numerical errors being tested
records.text:
The input is a simple-cubic cell of side 4 bohr containing one He atom at the origin. A local GTH–PADE pseudopotential supplies two valence electrons for a closed-shell, spin-unpolarized Kohn–Sham problem. This He potential has no nonlocal projectors. One example therefore does not validate general multielement crystals or nonlocal pseudopotentials. The geometry is fixed as a teaching configuration for convergence experiments.
The exchange-correlation functional is specified explicitly as Libxc LDA_X plus LDA_C_VWN (VWN5). The label LDA alone does not align choices such as VWN and Perdew–Wang correlation. GTH–PADE names the chosen pseudopotential; it does not assert that its generation approximation is identical to the VWN5 used here. Both engines receive the same pseudopotential coefficients and exchange-correlation choice.
Atomic units are used, with lattice lengths in bohr and energies in hartree. Total energies are compared per unit cell, including electronic terms and periodic ion–ion interactions. SCF solution error, k-point quadrature, the orbital basis and the auxiliary density/potential grid are varied separately. Reducing these numerical effects does not measure the physical error of LDA or the pseudopotential approximation.
\left[-\tfrac12\nabla^2+V_{\mathrm{loc}}+V_H[n]+V_{\mathrm{xc}}[n]\right]\psi_{n\mathbf k}=\varepsilon_{n\mathbf k}\psi_{n\mathbf k}

records.title: Periodic DFT: Γ points, k-point integration, basis sets, SCF and an independent reference
records.section: Bloch’s theorem and the units of a k point
records.text:
For a periodic potential, an orbital can be written as a plane-wave phase times a lattice-periodic function. The periodic function u and the Bloch orbital ψ are distinct: u is periodic across cell boundaries, whereas ψ satisfies a k-dependent phase boundary condition. Γ is the special point k=0, where this phase is one.
Here A contains direct lattice vectors as columns and B contains reciprocal vectors as columns, with AᵀB=2πI. Fractional coordinates κ give the physical wavevector k=Bκ. The coordinates κ are dimensionless; k is in bohr⁻¹ when the lattice is in bohr. PySCF stores cell vectors as rows and passes physical wavevectors to SCF. A shared input lattice and fractional k-point list prevent confusion with DFTK’s column convention.
\psi_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)=e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}u_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r),\qquad u_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r+\mathbf R)=u_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r),\qquad\psi_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r+\mathbf R)=e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf R}\psi_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)A=(\mathbf a_1,\mathbf a_2,\mathbf a_3),\qquad B=2\pi A^{-\mathsf T},\qquad\mathbf k=B\boldsymbol\kappa,\qquad\Omega=|\det A|
Sources: Felix Bloch (1929), PySCF developers (2026), DFTK developers (2026)

records.title: Periodic DFT: Γ points, k-point integration, basis sets, SCF and an independent reference
records.section: Γ points and k meshes: quadrature versus band paths
records.text:
Densities and energies of an infinite crystal involve integrals over the Brillouin zone. A finite set of k points and weights approximates these integrals. This example explicitly lists all points of a uniform mesh containing Γ and equal weights summing to one. Γ is included even for even subdivisions. This convention is not automatically identical to software defaults or the half-grid displacement of an even Monkhorst–Pack mesh. Fractional k points differing by an integer reciprocal vector represent the same point.
A Γ-only calculation is a one-point quadrature of the Brillouin zone. It can be adequate for some large real-space cells or localized orbitals, but adequacy for this small cell must be measured. Γ-only and several meshes are compared with the same orbital basis, auxiliary grid and SCF settings. Different meshes need not be nested, and monotonically decreasing energy differences are not assumed.
A band path joins high-symmetry points to visualize dispersion. Giving its points equal weights generally does not produce a Brillouin-zone quadrature. This example tests integrated energy and density; drawing a band path does not replace k-point convergence.

Actual calculations are three-dimensional.\frac{1}{|\mathrm{BZ}|}\int_{\mathrm{BZ}}f(\mathbf k)\,d\mathbf k\simeq\sum_{q=1}^{N_k}w_qf(\mathbf k_q),\qquad\sum_qw_q=1,\qquad n(\mathbf r)=2\sum_qw_q\sum_{n\in\mathrm{occ}}|\psi_{n\mathbf k_q}(\mathbf r)|^2\boldsymbol\kappa_{\mathbf j}=\left(\frac{j_1}{N_1},\frac{j_2}{N_2},\frac{j_3}{N_3}\right)\bmod\mathbb Z^3,\quad j_i=0,\ldots,N_i-1,\quad w_{\mathbf j}=\frac{1}{N_1N_2N_3}
Sources: H. J. Monkhorst and J. D. Pack (1976), PySCF developers (2026)

records.title: Periodic DFT: Γ points, k-point integration, basis sets, SCF and an independent reference
records.section: The orbital basis and auxiliary FFT grid are separate convergence axes
records.text:
The PySCF orbitals expand Bloch sums of Gaussian functions. Results retain basis names such as gth-dzv, the actual function count and overlap conditioning. Increasing a basis’s zeta label does not prove a complete-basis limit; bases with different contractions and polarization functions are not necessarily mathematically nested. Basis differences measure sensitivity within the published finite sequence.
FFT density fitting (FFTDF) is an auxiliary plane-wave/FFT representation used for quantities such as density and Coulomb potentials. Refining its mesh does not enlarge the Gaussian orbital space. Conversely, enlarging only the orbital basis cannot remove errors from a coarse auxiliary grid. The PySCF auxiliary grid, DFTK orbital plane-wave cutoff and its associated density grid are distinct, and hartree must not be confused with rydberg.
The periodic Coulomb G=0 component is handled with a convention combining electrons, the local pseudopotential and periodic ionic terms. A change in the mean potential also shifts the orbital eigenvalue origin. Even the same physical model needs aligned G=0 constants, pseudopotential corrections, Ewald terms and per-cell versus per-atom units for direct total-energy comparison. Conventions and energy components are checked rather than adding an empirical constant to force agreement.

records.title: Periodic DFT: Γ points, k-point integration, basis sets, SCF and an independent reference
records.section: SCF residuals, electron count and a sampled KS gap
records.text:
The Kohn–Sham potential depends on density, so an eigenproblem and density update are iterated. Energy changes are supplemented by a commutator residual built from the final density, orbital-equation residuals, orthogonality and electron count. The commutator measure is the maximum over k points of the Frobenius norm of X(FPS−SPF)X, with symmetric orthogonalization X=S⁻¹ᐟ². Orbital residuals use the same final-density F. Results retain iteration histories, stopping reasons and tolerances. Reaching an iteration cap is not labeled convergence.
A tolerance sweep changes only SCF settings at fixed discretization and measures the energy difference from a tight solution. This checks the remaining nonlinear solution error. SCF convergence is separate from sufficient orbital bases, auxiliary grids and k points, and from physical-model accuracy.

records.title: Periodic DFT: Γ points, k-point integration, basis sets, SCF and an independent reference
records.section: Comparison with an independent DFTK reference in a different basis
records.text:
The example uses PySCF’s periodic integrals, FFTDF and SCF. The independent Julia package DFTK supplies a plane-wave Kohn–Sham reference without calling the teaching PySCF solver. Merely changing an auxiliary representation within PySCF would not be an independent-implementation comparison. Both engines use Libxc for exchange-correlation evaluation, so that component is not independently implemented in this comparison.
The lattice, atomic positions, valence count, spin, pseudopotential coefficients, LDA_X plus LDA_C_VWN, fractional k points and weights are aligned. Plane-wave cutoff and SCF convergence are checked on the DFTK side. Gaussian and plane-wave calculations use different finite spaces, so machine-precision agreement is not demanded between their finite-basis energies. Agreement is assessed against the published acceptance width alongside Gaussian-basis and auxiliary-grid sensitivities and reference-cutoff dependence. Meeting this width establishes neither a rigorous bound on true error nor chemical accuracy.

records.title: Periodic DFT: Γ points, k-point integration, basis sets, SCF and an independent reference
records.section: First-principles MD: Born–Oppenheimer and Car–Parrinello methods
records.text:
First-principles molecular dynamics (AIMD) moves nuclei using electronic-structure calculations. Born–Oppenheimer molecular dynamics (BOMD) converges the electronic ground state at each nuclear configuration, then integrates classical nuclear motion using forces on that energy surface. E_BO below includes ionic interactions. The 1927 Born–Oppenheimer paper is cited for electronic–nuclear separation, not as the publication of a modern BOMD program.
In BOMD, SCF tolerances must control forces and trajectory reproducibility as well as energies. Atom-centered finite Gaussian bases require force contributions from basis-position dependence (Pulay terms). Finite-difference force checks, timestep refinement and energy drift in unthermostatted NVE trajectories are separate tests. Predicting an electronic initial guess does not remove the requirement to optimize each configuration to adequate accuracy.
Car–Parrinello molecular dynamics (CPMD) propagates nuclear coordinates and electronic orbitals together through an extended Lagrangian. The fictitious orbital mass μ is a numerical parameter, rather than the physical electron mass. Lagrange multipliers Λ enforce orthonormality. The displayed convention uses a μ/2 orbital-velocity term at fixed cell and occupations. Generalization to periodic k sampling must consistently include weights and occupations in electronic terms.

records.title: Periodic DFT: Γ points, k-point integration, basis sets, SCF and an independent reference
records.section: First-principles MD: Born–Oppenheimer and Car–Parrinello methods
records.text:
CPMD orbital propagation does not represent real electronic excitations as in TDDFT. Electronic fictitious motion must remain separated in timescale from nuclear motion, keeping orbitals near the BO surface. Vary μ, timestep and orthogonality tolerance while monitoring fictitious kinetic energy and energy transfer to nuclei. Distinguish the ideal unthermostatted extended-system conserved energy E_ext from nuclear kinetic plus BO energy. These statements do not establish applicability to narrow-gap systems or metals.
This section is reading only. This chapter’s fixed one-atom He example validates static total energies and k-point, basis, auxiliary-grid and SCF convergence. Multiatom He forces, energy finite differences, an independent reference and the BOMD force interface are covered in the separate From DFT to atomic forces chapter and release. Long BOMD/CPMD trajectories, timestep/SCF/fictitious-mass sensitivity and thermostats require separate validation.
A separate fixed-input educational example executes a short, dimensionless two-state electronic-angle/nuclear-coordinate BO/CP-type model. It does not propagate this chapter’s periodic He calculation or establish general Kohn–Sham BOMD/CPMD, real-material or long-time MD validation.

records.title: From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface
records.section: Forces are negative gradients of the total energy
records.text:
For a fixed lattice, electron count, functional and pseudopotential, the electronic ground state is solved at each atomic configuration. The Born–Oppenheimer energy is the total cell energy, including electronic and periodic ion–ion terms. The force on Cartesian component α of atom I is minus the total derivative with respect to that coordinate. Gradient and force signs must be distinguished: coordinates in bohr and energies in hartree give forces in hartree/bohr.
The input is a cubic cell of side 5 bohr with He positions (0.37, 0.61, 0.83) and (2.13, 2.27, 2.41) bohr: four valence electrons in a closed-shell fixed configuration. It avoids a check in which symmetry makes every force zero. Directions and all x, y and z components are compared, as well as magnitudes. Numerical agreement for this artificial arrangement does not predict an equilibrium helium crystal or establish chemical accuracy. Stress and pressure require cell derivatives, separate from atomic-position derivatives at fixed cell.
E_{\mathrm{BO}}(\mathbf R;A)=\min_{\langle\psi_i|\psi_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}}E_{\mathrm{KS}}[\{\psi_i\};\mathbf R,A]F_{I\alpha}=-\left.\frac{d E_{\mathrm{BO}}}{dR_{I\alpha}}\right|_{A,N_e},\qquad [F_{I\alpha}]=E_h/a_0
Sources: M. Born and R. Oppenheimer (1927), R. P. Feynman (1939)

records.title: From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface
records.section: The Hellmann–Feynman theorem and Pulay terms from moving bases
records.text:
For a normalized exact eigenstate, the energy derivative with respect to a parameter equals the expectation of the Hamiltonian derivative. This is the Hellmann–Feynman relation. Feynman’s 1939 paper is a historical primary source for evaluating molecular forces directly. The theorem alone does not make every force correct for an electronic state represented in a finite atom-centered basis. The H and Ψ below express the general theorem; they do not replace the Kohn–Sham total energy by a sum of orbital eigenvalues.
A Gaussian basis moving with the atoms changes its functions and overlap matrix when nuclei move. Even with variationally optimized orbital coefficients, derivatives of this basis dependence must be included when differentiating the discrete energy. These are Pulay terms. The overlap derivative contracted with an energy-weighted density in the generalized eigenproblem is one contribution. The driver uses PySCF analytic nuclear gradients; it does not substitute a bare electron–ion Coulomb force.
At fixed cell and cutoff, plane waves do not move with atomic positions. Finite-cutoff force errors nevertheless remain, and SCF and density-grid errors must still be controlled. The absence of moving-atom basis terms does not make plane-wave forces exact. Basis changes under cell deformation and Pulay stress are distinct from this fixed-cell test.

records.title: From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface
records.section: The Hellmann–Feynman theorem and Pulay terms from moving bases
records.text:
H(\lambda)\Psi=E(\lambda)\Psi,\quad\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{dE}{d\lambda}=\left\langle\Psi\left|\frac{\partial H}{\partial\lambda}\right|\Psi\right\rangleF_{\mathbf k}C_{\mathbf k}=S_{\mathbf k}C_{\mathbf k}\varepsilon_{\mathbf k},\quad W_{\mathbf k}=C_{\mathbf k}f_{\mathbf k}\varepsilon_{\mathbf k}C_{\mathbf k}^{\dagger},\quad \left.\frac{dE}{dR_{I\alpha}}\right|_{\text{overlap term}}=-\sum_qw_q\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(W_{\mathbf k_q}\frac{\partial S_{\mathbf k_q}}{\partial R_{I\alpha}}\right)
Sources: R. P. Feynman (1939), P. Pulay (1969), PySCF developers (2026), DFTK developers (2026)

records.title: From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface
records.section: Finite-difference checks: smaller displacements are not always better
records.text:
One Cartesian component of one atom is displaced by ±h from the baseline configuration. At each displaced geometry the SCF is converged independently, and the resulting total energies give a central-difference force. The lattice, k points and weights, basis name, FFT grid, functional, pseudopotential and electron count are aligned. The atom-centered basis moves too, so this probes derivatives of the same discrete energy including basis-position dependence.
For a smooth energy surface, central-difference truncation is O(h²). SCF solution and roundoff errors in energies are divided by 2h, so very small displacements can increase errors. Several h values are retained to locate a stable agreement range with analytic forces. A clean U-shaped measured curve is not assumed. An input SCF energy tolerance is not interpreted as a rigorous bound on the error of each energy.
Agreement with finite differences from the same engine checks internal consistency, including signs, components and basis derivatives. Both use shared functional and pseudopotential implementations, so this alone is not an independent physical reference. A separate plane-wave DFTK implementation provides the independent comparison here.
F^{\mathrm{FD}}_{I\alpha}(h)=-\frac{E(\mathbf R+h\mathbf e_{I\alpha})-E(\mathbf R-h\mathbf e_{I\alpha})}{2h}F^{\mathrm{FD}}(h)-F=\mathcal O(h^2)+\mathcal O(\delta E/h)

records.title: From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface
records.section: Converge basis, k points, auxiliary grids and SCF for forces separately
records.text:
A small energy change alone does not establish converged forces. The Gaussian orbital basis, Brillouin-zone mesh, auxiliary FFT grid and SCF stopping conditions are varied one at a time, comparing forces on the same atoms and Cartesian components. Atom ordering and axes are fixed. Summaries use an L∞-type maximum absolute component norm, distinct from a per-atom vector magnitude or a component average.
Increasing a basis’s zeta label does not necessarily produce nested spaces or monotonic force changes. Nor are all k meshes nested. The final pair of settings is compared with a published target, without presenting the increment as a rigorous complete-basis or infinite-k-point error bound. The auxiliary FFT representation of density and local potentials is a separate convergence axis from the Gaussian orbital space.
Incomplete SCF convergence also affects forces. Alongside termination flags and iteration counts, inspect stored electron-count, orbital and SCF residual diagnostics. Force sensitivity to tighter stopping conditions is measured directly, and an unconverged electronic state must not be returned to BOMD as an accepted force.

records.title: From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface
records.section: Independent reference: the same model in a different discretization
records.text:
PySCF uses a periodic Gaussian basis and FFTDF; the reference uses DFTK’s plane-wave Hamiltonian, SCF, periodic ion interactions and analytic forces. Lattice and all atomic positions, valence count, spin restriction and integer occupations, every local-GTH coefficient, Libxc LDA_X plus LDA_C_VWN (VWN5), fractional k points and weights are matched. No fitted energy offset or force correction is applied.
The DFTK plane-wave cutoff is increased separately and its final force increment is measured. This is not a rounding-error comparison of identical finite matrices. Different finite Gaussian and plane-wave spaces are assessed using the published acceptance width and convergence diagnostics on both sides. Both engines share Libxc, which limits the extent of implementation independence.
DFTK compute_forces returns a representation associated with fractional coordinates; the Cartesian API is compute_forces_cart. Coordinate and force transformations are different. Comparisons here use Cartesian components in hartree/bohr throughout. The generation script, pinned Julia environment, pseudopotential, input and result hashes are retained. Comparing against the saved reference in Python and regenerating the reference in Julia are distinct operations.
\mathbf R=A\boldsymbol\xi,\qquad \mathbf F_{\mathrm{cart}}=-A^{-\mathsf T}\nabla_{\boldsymbol\xi}E

records.title: From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface
records.section: Check components, translation and nonzero forces
records.text:
A configuration with nearly zero forces can pass even with a sign error. A multiatom configuration carrying nonzero forces is used, with componentwise comparisons of analytic forces, finite differences and the independent reference. A single force norm should not hide component permutations, atom-order mistakes or incorrect units.
In an ideal periodic system without external fields, uniform translation leaves the total energy unchanged and the sum of atomic forces vanishes. Finite real-space grids can numerically break this property; the remaining total force is a useful grid and differentiation diagnostic. Translation checks alone do not establish accurate relative forces, so energy differences and an independent reference are used alongside them.
E(\{\mathbf R_I+\mathbf t\})=E(\{\mathbf R_I\})\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\sum_I\mathbf F_I=\mathbf 0
Sources: DFTK developers (2026), PySCF developers (2026)

records.title: From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface
records.section: The BOMD interface and additional trajectory validation
records.text:
The BOMD force provider energy_and_forces accepts positions_bohr and returns energy_per_cell and forces_cartesian from the same energy surface, together with SCF convergence and residual diagnostics. An unconverged electronic state is treated as a failure. Masses belong to nuclear time integration, not as factors multiplying the DFT potential energy or forces. Wrapped positions inside a periodic cell must be distinguished from a continuous trajectory record.
Velocity Verlet advances velocities by half a step, updates positions, solves the electronic problem again for the new forces, then completes the velocity update. Carrying an electronic guess from a previous step accelerates the calculation but does not replace SCF convergence. This verification focuses on atomic forces and the BOMD handoff; a single force evaluation or short interface smoke test is not counted as validation of long trajectories.
Accepting a practical trajectory additionally requires timestep refinement, tighter-SCF comparisons, total-energy and momentum checks in unthermostatted NVE, and time-reversal checks where appropriate. Thermostats can hide force or integration errors by absorbing energy changes, so unthermostatted checks come first. Small short-time drift does not guarantee long-time stability or a correct statistical distribution.

records.title: From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface
records.section: The BOMD interface and additional trajectory validation
records.text:
Car–Parrinello dynamics is a distinct formulation propagating fictitious electronic degrees of freedom alongside nuclei. A force provider on the Born–Oppenheimer surface is not a CPMD implementation. The cross-field navigation separately shows the executed scope of DFT, force evaluation, nuclear integration and temperature control.
The method registry also links a separate two-state BO/CP-type educational model. Its fixed inputs are distinct from this chapter’s He2 forces/local Verlet interface; neither example establishes general Kohn–Sham trajectories, real materials or long-time MD.
\mathbf v_{n+1/2}=\mathbf v_n+\frac{\Delta t}{2M}\mathbf F(\mathbf R_n),\quad\mathbf R_{n+1}=\mathbf R_n+\Delta t\,\mathbf v_{n+1/2},\quad\mathbf v_{n+1}=\mathbf v_{n+1/2}+\frac{\Delta t}{2M}\mathbf F(\mathbf R_{n+1})\mathcal E_n=E_{\mathrm{BO}}(\mathbf R_n)+\sum_I\frac{M_I}{2}|\mathbf v_{I,n}|^2,\qquad \Delta\mathcal E_n=\mathcal E_n-\mathcal E_0
Sources: M. Born and R. Oppenheimer (1927), J. M. Herbert and M. Head-Gordon (2005), R. Car and M. Parrinello (1985)

records.title: Particle-in-cell / PIC
records.section: Particle-in-cell / PIC
records.text: Plasma PIC represents a distribution by computational particles and self-consistent fields by a mesh. Its smoothing, collisionality and sampling error differ from direct all-pairs Coulomb dynamics.

records.title: Particle-in-cell / PIC
records.section: Problem and representative equations
records.text:
Start with nonrelativistic electrostatic Vlasov–Poisson. Computational particle p has weight wₚ, charge qₚ and position xₚ. Dimensionless shape weights Sᵢ sum to one, and Vᵢ is cell volume. Deposit ρ, solve Poisson with the stated boundary conditions, and use E=−∇φ.
\rho_i=\frac1{V_i}\sum_p w_pq_pS_i(\mathbf x_p),\qquad -\nabla_h^2\phi_i=\rho_i/\epsilon_0,\qquad \dot{\mathbf v}_p=(q_p/m_p)\mathbf E_h(\mathbf x_p).

records.title: Particle-in-cell / PIC
records.section: Algorithm
records.text: Repeat charge deposition, field solution, particle gathering and particle pushing; include background ions in ρ. Electromagnetic PIC additionally needs current deposition and Maxwell updates consistent with discrete continuity. Dawson’s sheet model is a historical particle-plasma example, not the definition of every PIC discretization.

records.title: Particle-in-cell / PIC
records.section: Conditions and pitfalls
records.text:
Explicit electrostatic PIC must examine plasma-frequency time scales and Debye-length resolution. Exact restrictions depend on the particle pusher, shape and field solver. Separate sampling convergence in particle count from grid/time convergence, and check self-force and finite-grid heating.
The companion is one-dimensional periodic electrostatic cold-electron PIC with a fixed uniform ion background. It is a fixed CIC deposit/gather, Poisson-field and particle-push example; thermal Landau damping, electromagnetic PIC and moving ions are outside its scope.

records.title: Particle-in-cell / PIC
records.section: What to check
records.text:
Begin with single-particle self-force, a uniform neutral distribution, and small-amplitude plasma oscillations or Landau damping. Report charge, energy drift, particle-count dependence and independent random realizations. Compare damping rates only within the linear-amplitude regime used by the theory.
Use linear cold-plasma oscillation as a small-amplitude reference and vary mesh, time step and particle count separately. Report charge, field residual, self-force, particle momentum and particle-plus-field energy diagnostics separately. Small conservation diagnostics alone guarantee neither trajectory accuracy nor arbitrary long-time stability.
The companion also integrates the fixed CIC spatial system with DOP853 and tests tolerance/maximum-step sensitivity. This is an alternative time-integration algorithm, not an independent continuum Vlasov–Poisson solver. The random particle-count check concerns the initial power of one Fourier charge mode, compared with its analytic expectation including the finite-grid CIC response. It is distinct from particle-count convergence of arbitrary nonlinear trajectories.

records.title: PINNs and neural operators
records.section: PINNs and neural operators
records.text: A PINN fits a neural representation of a particular solution; a neural operator learns a map from input functions such as coefficients or initial data to solution functions. Their targets and validation protocols differ.

records.title: PINNs and neural operators
records.section: Problem and representative equations
records.text:
A PINN minimizes an empirical weighted loss of PDE, boundary and data residuals. N and B are differential/boundary operators and f,g are prescribed data. A representative FNO layer combines a Fourier-parameterized integral operator K with a local map W acting on feature functions v.
\mathcal L(\theta)=\lambda_r\langle|\mathcal N[u_\theta]-f|^2\rangle_r+\lambda_b\langle|\mathcal B[u_\theta]-g|^2\rangle_b+\lambda_d\langle|u_\theta-u_{\rm obs}|^2\rangle_d.v_{\ell+1}=\sigma\!\left(W_\ell v_\ell+\mathcal F^{-1}[K_\ell\,\mathcal Fv_\ell]\right).

records.title: PINNs and neural operators
records.section: Algorithm
records.text: For a PINN, scale coordinates/units, differentiate residuals, specify collocation points and boundary enforcement, and optimize. FNO trains an operator on input/reference-solution pairs and truncates Fourier modes. Cite the PINN and FNO papers as separate proposals.

records.title: PINNs and neural operators
records.section: Conditions and pitfalls
records.text: Small training loss is not a bound on global solution error or conservation. Examine residual imbalance, shocks, stiff scales and out-of-distribution inputs. Transfer between discretizations is not a guarantee of physical correctness at arbitrary resolution.

records.title: PINNs and neural operators
records.section: What to check
records.text: Compare against analytic or independently converged conventional solutions. Measure off-training L1/L2/L∞ errors, boundaries, conservation and multiple seeds. Split operator data by independent problems rather than nearby time slices alone, and report distribution-shift tests separately.

records.title: PINNs and neural operators
records.section: Selected original sources and the present small examples
records.text: Selected section 2 of the 2017 PINN Part I preprint distinguishes residual loss from data and boundary losses. Sections 3–4 of FNO version 3 (2021) combine a local linear map, a Fourier integral map and nonlinear activation. The present small Poisson and periodic-heat inputs are separate educational choices. Neither the full 2019 JCP article nor the original large experiments or performance claims are reproduced.

records.title: Particle mesh Ewald / PME
records.section: Particle mesh Ewald / PME
records.text: PME transfers the reciprocal Ewald calculation to a mesh and uses FFTs. Distinguish the original Lagrange-interpolation PME from the later B-spline construction of SPME.

records.title: Particle mesh Ewald / PME
records.section: Problem and representative equations
records.text:
For a neutral triply periodic Coulomb system, Qₘ is charge assigned to mesh point xₘ using weights Wₘ. The reciprocal operator Ĝₕ includes Ewald screening, mesh conventions and interpolation corrections. This schematic describes only the reciprocal contribution; real-space and self terms remain necessary.
Q_{\mathbf m}=\sum_iq_iW_{\mathbf m}(\mathbf r_i),\qquad\phi_h=\mathcal F_h^{-1}\!\left[\widehat G_h\,\mathcal F_h Q\right].

records.title: Particle mesh Ewald / PME
records.section: Algorithm
records.text: Assign charges with local Lagrange polynomials, transform the mesh, apply the reciprocal convolution and transform back. Specify the differentiation and particle-gather rules together. A mesh-interpolated field and the derivative of the discrete energy need not give identical forces.

records.title: Particle mesh Ewald / PME
records.section: Conditions and pitfalls
records.text:
Separate mesh resolution, interpolation order, Ewald cutoffs and force differentiation in error studies. State FFT normalization, k=0 treatment and units. The usual O(N log N) description assumes an appropriate mesh-growth regime and is not an accuracy guarantee.
The linked implementation adopts smooth PME with B-spline analytical energy gradients. It does not implement or validate the original 1993 Lagrange-interpolation PME; the original PME equations, sources and applicability remain distinct from this implemented variant.

records.title: Particle mesh Ewald / PME
records.section: What to check
records.text:
Use a converged direct Ewald calculation for the identical neutral cell. Vary mesh size, interpolation order and screening; measure RMS/maximum energy and force errors and sensitivity to common translations. A gravity-PM test does not validate PME.
The companion varies mesh size, B-spline order and common translation for the same neutral periodic charges, comparing against converged direct Ewald and a separately implemented theta integral. The direct-Ewald comparison shares real-space/self terms, so agreement there alone is not independent validation of the entire energy.
