records.title: QR, SVD and least squares
records.section: QR, SVD and least squares
records.text: Least squares, low-rank approximation and conditioning call for different matrix decompositions. QR reduces a problem to orthogonal transformations and a triangular solve; SVD exposes singular values and resolvable directions.

records.title: QR, SVD and least squares
records.section: Problem and representative equations
records.text:
For a real m×n matrix with m≥n, thin QR has QᵀQ=I and upper triangular R. Full column rank gives the least-squares solve Rx=Qᵀb. SVD has nonnegative singular values σᵢ. Truncating small σᵢ in a pseudoinverse regularizes the problem and can change the solution being sought.
A=QR=U\Sigma V^T,\qquad \min_x\|Ax-b\|_2,\qquad A^+b=\sum_{\sigma_i>\tau}\frac{u_i^Tb}{\sigma_i}v_i\quad\text{(truncated)}.

records.title: QR, SVD and least squares
records.section: Algorithm
records.text: Householder QR eliminates subdiagonal entries with reflections and generally maintains orthogonality better than classical Gram–Schmidt. Consider column pivoting or SVD for rank diagnosis. Classical SVD algorithms reduce to bidiagonal form using orthogonal transformations rather than explicitly forming normal equations.

records.title: QR, SVD and least squares
records.section: Conditions and pitfalls
records.text:
For full column rank, κ₂(AᵀA)=κ₂(A)². A small residual can coexist with uncertain coefficients under ill-conditioning or noise. Choose a numerical-rank threshold relative to scale, rounding and measurement uncertainty, and consider column scaling when variables have different units.
Distinguish residual/backward error from forward errors in coefficients or singular values. At large condition numbers, small changes to the input or right-hand side can cause large coefficient changes. Numerical rank depends on a singular-value threshold and arithmetic precision; a truncated least-squares solution need not solve the original problem exactly.
General least-squares sensitivity also depends on the angle between the right-hand side and the column space, not only on condition number. Published relative-accuracy results for one-sided Jacobi SVD depend on stopping rules and componentwise conditioning. Agreement for small singular values in these small matrices is not a universal relative-accuracy guarantee for arbitrary ill-conditioned matrices.

records.title: QR, SVD and least squares
records.section: What to check
records.text:
Check relative factorization residuals, orthogonality and Aᵀ(Ax−b). Test prescribed singular values and rank-deficient cases, and compare solution changes under controlled data perturbations.
The added release compares errors across small matrices with prescribed singular values, fixed right-hand-side perturbations and numerical-rank thresholds. Measure QR/SVD reconstruction and orthogonality, least-squares residual, coefficient forward error and numerical rank separately. Distinguish LAPACK references from independent high-precision references constructed from the actual binary floating-point input. Condition-number squaring for normal equations is explained above as theory; it is not an executed control in this added case.

records.title: Gaussian and adaptive quadrature
records.section: Gaussian and adaptive quadrature
records.text: Gaussian quadrature selects nodes and weights for a measure to integrate polynomials efficiently. Adaptive integration separately allocates function evaluations using local error estimates.

records.title: Gaussian and adaptive quadrature
records.section: Problem and representative equations
records.text:
For a positive measure, an n-point Gaussian rule is exact through degree 2n−1 when the required moments exist. The Jacobi matrix J of orthogonal-polynomial recurrence coefficients has quadrature nodes as eigenvalues. Weights are μ₀ times squared first components of normalized eigenvectors, with μ₀=∫w.
\int_a^b f(x)w(x)\,dx\approx\sum_{j=1}^n\omega_jf(x_j),\qquad Jv_j=x_jv_j,\quad\omega_j=\mu_0(v_j)_1^2.

records.title: Gaussian and adaptive quadrature
records.section: Algorithm
records.text: Golub–Welsch solves this symmetric tridiagonal eigenproblem. Adaptive Gauss–Kronrod-type integration uses differences between nested rules to estimate local errors, subdivides intervals and checks absolute/relative tolerances. The rule difference is not an unconditional error bound.

records.title: Gaussian and adaptive quadrature
records.section: Conditions and pitfalls
records.text:
Singularities, jumps, rapid oscillations and narrow peaks can be missed by sampled nodes. Split at known discontinuities and consider transformations or matched weighted rules. Relative tolerance alone is unsuitable when the integral is close to zero.
When cancellation makes an integral small, a cancellation condition number such as integral(|f|)/|integral(f)| is informative. Absolute/relative true errors differ from a rule’s internal error estimate. If finitely many sample points miss a narrow bump, agreement between two approximations can coexist with a large true integration error. State the input-perturbation norm and perturbation model when comparing condition numbers; if the integral is zero, relative condition and relative error are undefined, so report absolute quantities.

records.title: Gaussian and adaptive quadrature
records.section: What to check
records.text:
Verify degree of exactness on monomials, then test nonpolynomials with known integrals, singularities and narrow peaks. Record estimated versus true error, evaluation count and termination caused by subdivision limits.
The added release varies rule order and tolerance for smooth functions with known integrals, cancellation-sensitive functions and a fixed narrow-bump control. Compare against independent references and record true error, estimated error and function evaluations separately. Distinguish an explicitly split calculation that resolves the bump from a missed-bump diagnostic; neither supplies a universal guarantee for all integrands. Compare an endpoint-derivative singularity before and after a change of variables, and retain evaluation/depth-budget exhaustion as an explicit termination status.

Computation for a fixed target
Construct Gaussian nodes/weights from the Legendre recurrence and test polynomial moments through degree 2n−1 and an exponential. Adaptive Simpson integrates exponential and Lorentzian peaks, against analytic integrals and independent QUADPACK.
The local Simpson estimate is not a rigorous error bound for arbitrary functions. The implementation does not generally solve missed high frequencies, singularities or roundoff stagnation, and it is not a reimplementation of Gauss–Kronrod or all of QUADPACK.

Eigensolvers, SCF, mixing and DIIS: how accurately is the chosen discrete problem solved?

records.title: Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations
records.section: Schrodinger eigenproblems
records.text:
The common starting point is a many-electron eigenproblem at fixed nuclear positions. We use nonrelativistic Born–Oppenheimer theory and atomic units, separating electronic energy E_el from nuclear repulsion E_NN. R_A and Z_A denote nuclear positions and charges; r_ij is an electron–electron distance.
For one electron the pair-repulsion sum vanishes; hydrogenic energies E_n = −Z²/(2n²) provide references. The many-electron wavefunction depends on all electronic coordinates and spins, unlike the individual three-dimensional orbitals in HF or KS.
Uniform radial-grid tests of isolated hydrogenic 1s, 2s, 2p and 3d states; not a direct general many-electron Schrödinger solver. Fixed inputs, code and measured checks
\hat H_{\rm el}=-\frac12\sum_i\nabla_i^2-\sum_{iA}\frac{Z_A}{|\mathbf r_i-\mathbf R_A|}+\sum_{i<j}\frac1{r_{ij}}\hat H_{\rm el}\Psi=E_{\rm el}\Psi,\qquad E_{\rm tot}=E_{\rm el}+\sum_{A<B}\frac{Z_AZ_B}{R_{AB}}
Long equations scroll horizontally.
Nuclear dynamics, relativity, spin–orbit coupling and external fields are outside this representative Hamiltonian. A small eigenpair residual does not establish domain or basis convergence.
Assumptions, implementation status and JSON

Roothaan, C. C. J. (1951)

records.title: Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations
records.section: Hartree–Fock
records.text:
HF makes the energy stationary within single antisymmetric Slater determinants. Exchange follows from the determinant; electron correlation relative to the HF reference is absent. Closed-shell RHF builds its Fock operator from doubly occupied spatial orbitals.
J_j is a Coulomb operator and K_j is generally nonlocal exchange. Open-shell choices include UHF and ROHF, with spin contamination and symmetry breaking requiring explicit diagnostics.
Only spherical helium with one doubly occupied 1s spatial orbital; the local HF exchange reduction is specific to this two-electron problem. A separate edition adds H₂ RHF in finite s-Gaussian bases. Fixed inputs, code and measured checks
New H₂ closed-shell RHF example: original s-Gaussian integrals, independent PySCF comparisons, SCF residuals and basis refinement. Limited to finite s-type subspaces; does not validate general molecules, molecular DFT, periodic systems or correct dissociation. H₂ inputs, code, independent references and refinement
\hat F=\hat h+\sum_{j\in\mathrm{occ}}(2\hat J_j-\hat K_j),\qquad \hat F\phi_i=\varepsilon_i\phi_i\mathbf F\mathbf C=\mathbf S\mathbf C\boldsymbol\varepsilon,\qquad \mathbf C^\dagger\mathbf S\mathbf C=\mathbf I
Long equations scroll horizontally.

records.title: Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations
records.section: Kohn–Sham density functional theory / DFT
records.text:
Here DFT means density functional theory, rather than the discrete Fourier transform. Within the Hohenberg–Kohn ground-state framework, Kohn–Sham theory represents the density using auxiliary noninteracting orbitals. State the spin convention for occupations f_i and enforce their sum N.
T_s is the auxiliary kinetic energy and E_H the classical Coulomb energy. E_xc includes exchange, correlation and the difference between interacting kinetic energy and T_s. Updating density to potential and orbitals back to density produces the nonlinear SCF problem.
The representative local KS equation below assumes a differentiable density functional. Distinguish generalized KS treatments of nonlocal hybrid exchange and orbital-dependent meta-GGAs.
Spin-unpolarized exchange-only Dirac LDA for spherical helium; correlation, GGA, hybrids, molecules, periodic systems and excitations are not implemented. Fixed inputs, code and measured checks
Periodic KS-DFT for one fixed simple-cubic He cell. An educational PySCF workflow separately checks Gamma/k sampling, Gaussian orbital basis, auxiliary FFT grid and SCF tolerances against independent DFTK plane waves with identical GTH parameters and LDA exchange plus VWN5 correlation. Does not validate equilibrium helium solids, general materials or metals. Periodic DFT conditions, code, convergence and independent reference

SCF is an iteration for self-consistency in HF or KS, rather than a physical model. The map M builds a potential from the input density, solves for orbitals and constructs an output density.

records.title: Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations
records.section: Pulay / DIIS acceleration
records.text:
DIIS determines extrapolation coefficients from stored iterates and error vectors. Its basic form minimizes the extrapolated error norm subject to coefficients summing to one. SCF commonly uses Fock matrices and an overlap-consistent commutator residual.
It changes the nonlinear solution strategy rather than the physical approximation. Compare against damping using the same initial state and stopping rules; record history length and treatment of singular history matrices.
\min_{\{c_j\}}\left\|\sum_j c_j\mathbf e_j\right\|^2,\qquad \sum_j c_j=1
Extrapolation guarantees neither convergence nor monotonic energy decrease. Investigate initial-state dependence and unstable stationary solutions even when a residual appears small.

records.title: Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations
records.section: Coulomb and Hartree potentials
records.text:
With n defined as positive electron number density, the Hartree potential is the positive Coulomb integral below. Its sign differs from charge density ρ_charge = −n. Distinguish v_H in the electronic energy from electrostatic potential generated by charge.
Isolated systems require far-field conditions. Periodic systems require a stated G=0 convention, neutrality, compensating background when used, and potential reference. Existing Poisson, FFT and particle-force methods must be matched to these signs and boundaries.
Cumulative Coulomb quadrature for isolated spherical densities, checked against analytic exponential densities; not a general 3D or periodic Poisson implementation. Fixed inputs, code and measured checks
v_H(\mathbf r)=\int\frac{n(\mathbf r\prime)}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r\prime|}\,d\mathbf r\prime,\qquad \nabla^2v_H=-4\pi nE_H=\frac12\int n(\mathbf r)v_H(\mathbf r)\,d\mathbf r
Long equations scroll horizontally.
Check the Poisson residual, integrated electron number, far-field behavior and the one-half double-counting factor separately. A charged periodic cell does not directly give an isolated-system energy.

Hartree, D. R. (1928)
Kohn, W.; Sham, L. J. (1965)

records.section: LDA, GGA and hybrid functionals
records.text:
LDA depends on local density, GGA on density and its gradient, and meta-GGA on quantities such as orbital kinetic-energy density. Hybrids mix in HF-type exchange. PBE, SCAN, B3 variants and PBE0 are approximation choices rather than a universal ranking.
The formula below is spin-unpolarized Dirac exchange only. Distinguish it from LDA including correlation. State functional components, parameters, library/version and the density integration grid.
Only spin-unpolarized Dirac exchange energy and its functional derivative are verified; LDA correlation, GGA, meta-GGA and hybrids remain reading-only. Fixed inputs, code and measured checks

records.title: Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations
records.section: Band symmetry groups and irreducible representations
records.text:
A structural space group includes translations, rotations, mirrors, inversion and their combinations. Band classification must use the symmetries actually preserved by the Hamiltonian, including magnetic order, spin–orbit coupling (SOC) and external fields.
A Seitz operation g = {R|τ} maps position to Rr + τ. With lattice translations T as a normal subgroup, G/T is the crystal point group. At each k, the little group G_k retains operations taking Rk back to k modulo a reciprocal vector K. Its little co-group G_k/T is distinct from the full crystal point group.
g=\{R|\boldsymbol\tau\}:\ \mathbf r\mapsto R\mathbf r+\boldsymbol\tau,\qquad P=G/TG_{\mathbf k}=\{\{R|\boldsymbol\tau\}\in G:\ R\mathbf k=\mathbf k+\mathbf K,\ \mathbf K\in L^*\}
Long equations scroll horizontally.

records.title: Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations
records.section: Read little-group irreps and degeneracies
records.text:
Symmetries act within the Bloch-state space associated with k. Irreducible small representations classify bands. Their dimensions constrain symmetry-required multiplicities; accidental coincidence and antiunitary pairing are additional possibilities. Nearly equal energies alone do not identify an irrep.
Little groups change between high-symmetry points, lines and planes. Compatibility relations track representation branching and band connectivity. For a simple symmorphic mirror line without SOC, mirror eigenvalues +1 and −1 label distinct sectors that cannot hybridize while that symmetry is preserved.

records.title: Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations
records.section: Screw axes, glide planes and nonsymmorphic groups
records.text:
Screw and glide operations include fractional translations. Bloch phases matter, particularly at zone boundaries, so ordinary crystal-point-group character tables are insufficient. Use little-group small representations or equivalent projective little-co-group representations with their factor systems.
Nonsymmorphic symmetry can constrain degeneracies and connectivity. It does not imply that every band is degenerate at every k: specify the group, k, spin and time-reversal conditions.
\psi_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r+\mathbf a)=e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf a}\psi_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r),\qquad \mathbf a\in L

records.title: Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations
records.section: SOC, double groups, time reversal and Kramers pairs
records.text:
Spin-1/2 SOC requires spinors that change sign under a 2π rotation, hence double-valued representations of double groups. Time reversal Θ is antiunitary with Θ² = −1 for electrons. Time reversal alone generally pairs k with −k; Kramers degeneracy at the same k is guaranteed at time-reversal-invariant momenta (TRIM), where 2k is reciprocal.
In the usual nonmagnetic spin-1/2 setting with both inversion P and time reversal Θ, PΘ preserves each k and squares to −1, producing double degeneracy at each k. This conclusion cannot be transferred unchanged to a noncentrosymmetric system. Spinless Θ² = +1 models also do not satisfy these Kramers assumptions.
Magnetic order may break time reversal or retain only its combination with a spatial operation. Magnetic space groups and antiunitary corepresentations require separate treatment. Reassess symmetry settings whenever SOC or magnetic state changes.
\Theta H(\mathbf k)\Theta^{-1}=H(-\mathbf k),\qquad \Theta^2=-1\mathbf k_{\rm TRIM}=-\mathbf k_{\rm TRIM}+\mathbf K,\qquad \mathbf K\in L^*

records.title: Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations
records.section: Distinguish plotted paths from irreducible-zone integration
records.text:
Labels such as Γ, X, L and K and the chosen path depend on lattice, standardized cell and reciprocal-coordinate conventions. A plotted high-symmetry path is not an integration mesh. Band extrema may lie off the path, so it alone does not establish the global band gap.
Irreducible integration points and weights use the actual Hamiltonian symmetries and valid time reversal. Save lattice, positions/species, primitive/conventional-cell transformations, symmetry tolerances, SOC, magnetic and time-reversal settings, path/weights and software versions. Check sensitivity to structural rounding.
Bilbao supplies little-group representations; SeeK-path provides crystallographic paths; Quantum ESPRESSO bands.x documents lsym classification by little-group irreps. These links do not represent an atlas-verified band calculation or irrep assignment.

records.title: Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations
records.section: MP2 perturbation theory
records.text:
MP2 is a second-order perturbative correction to an HF reference. The representative expression uses canonical HF spin orbitals, occupied i,j, virtual a,b and antisymmetrized two-electron integrals. Coefficients and index conventions differ for restricted spatial-orbital formulas.
Match the basis, frozen core, reference orbitals, spin and nuclear geometry in comparisons. Save the correlation correction separately from total energy.
E_{\rm MP2}^{(2)}=\frac14\sum_{ij}^{\rm occ}\sum_{ab}^{\rm virt}\frac{|\langle ij\Vert ab\rangle|^2}{\varepsilon_i+\varepsilon_j-\varepsilon_a-\varepsilon_b}
Long equations scroll horizontally.
Small denominators and strong static correlation can invalidate low-order perturbation. An energy below HF is not by itself evidence of improvement toward the exact value.
Assumptions, implementation status and JSON
Møller, C.; Plesset, M. S. (1934)

records.title: Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations
records.section: Configuration interaction / CI
records.text:
CI diagonalizes the many-electron Hamiltonian in a space of determinants or configuration state functions. FCI spans the full chosen finite one-electron basis, electron number and symmetry sector; CISD truncates to single and double excitations from a reference.
Use FCI as a reference only with its finite-basis scope stated. Determinant spaces grow rapidly, motivating small validation systems such as H₂.
|\Psi\rangle=\sum_I c_I|\Phi_I\rangle,\qquad \sum_J H_{IJ}c_J=E c_I
Finite-basis FCI is not the exact continuum solution. Check size consistency of truncated CI and the assumptions behind variational bounds.
Assumptions, implementation status and JSON
Knowles, P. J.; Handy, N. C. (1984)

records.title: Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations
records.section: Coupled cluster / CCSD(T)
records.text:
Coupled cluster represents the wavefunction using an exponential excitation operator. CCSD iterates T₁+T₂; CCSD(T) conventionally adds a noniterative perturbative triples correction. It is distinct from CCSDT.
Assess whether a single determinant is adequate, using amplitude and reference diagnostics. Match frozen core, basis and reference state when comparing weakly correlated single-reference systems.
|\Psi_{\rm CC}\rangle=e^{\hat T}|\Phi_0\rangle,\qquad \hat T=\hat T_1+\hat T_2+\cdots
Conventional projected CC energies are not variational upper bounds. CCSD(T) is not a universal standard for bond breaking or strong correlation.
Assumptions, implementation status and JSON
Raghavachari, K.; Trucks, G. W.; Pople, J. A.; Head-Gordon, M. (1989)

records.title: Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations
records.section: CASSCF and multireference methods
records.text:
CASSCF optimizes configuration coefficients and orbitals within a selected active space. Record CAS(n_e,n_o), specifying electrons and spatial orbitals, their character, spin and any state averaging.
It addresses static correlation, but does not automatically recover adequate dynamic correlation outside the active space. Subsequent methods such as CASPT2 and NEVPT2 are separate future extensions.
|\Psi_{\rm CAS}\rangle=\sum_{I\in\operatorname{CAS}(n_e,n_o)}c_I|\Phi_I\rangle
Active-space dependence is distinct from grid error. Track orbital character across geometries rather than only orbital indices.
Assumptions, implementation status and JSON
Roos, B. O.; Taylor, P. R.; Siegbahn, P. E. M. (1980)

records.title: Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations
records.section: Time-dependent density functional theory / TDDFT
records.text:
TDDFT concerns time-dependent densities. The local time-dependent KS equation shown is representative; initial-state dependence and exchange-correlation memory can remain. Distinguish real-time propagation from linear response around a ground state.
For response calculations save excitation energies and oscillator strengths. For real time save the field, step size, propagation length and spectrum-transform settings. The adiabatic approximation concerns functional time dependence.
i\partial_t\phi_i(\mathbf r,t)=[-\tfrac12\nabla^2+v_s[n](\mathbf r,t)]\phi_i(\mathbf r,t)
Bare ground-state KS eigenvalue differences are not TDDFT excitation energies. Assess approximation limits for double excitations and long-range charge transfer.
Assumptions, implementation status and JSON
Runge, E.; Gross, E. K. U. (1984)

records.title: Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations
records.section: Quantum Monte Carlo
records.text:
VMC samples a trial-wavefunction variational energy; DMC projects toward the ground state through imaginary-time evolution. When using a fixed-node treatment of the fermion sign problem, identify its systematic bias.
Record random streams, autocorrelation-aware statistical uncertainty, time step, walker population, trial state and finite size. Ceperley–Alder electron-gas calculations also connect to LDA correlation.
E_{\rm VMC}=\frac{\int |\Psi_T|^2 E_L\,d\mathbf R}{\int |\Psi_T|^2\,d\mathbf R},\qquad E_L=\frac{\hat H\Psi_T}{\Psi_T}
Long equations scroll horizontally.
Statistical error bars do not capture fixed-node, time-step or finite-size bias. Quantum Monte Carlo here does not mean computation on a quantum computer.
Assumptions, implementation status and JSON
Ceperley, D. M.; Alder, B. J. (1980)

records.title: Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations
records.section: DMRG and tensor networks
records.text:
Quantum-chemical DMRG treats orbitals as sites and approximates many-electron states with representations such as matrix product states (MPS). Increasing bond dimension increases expressiveness; requirements also depend on orbital ordering and entanglement.
Record the active orbitals, ordering, bond dimension, sweeps, truncation measures and energy convergence. Access to larger correlated active spaces does not make arbitrary three-dimensional electronic-structure problems easy.
c_{n_1\cdots n_L}\approx\mathbf A_1^{n_1}\mathbf A_2^{n_2}\cdots\mathbf A_L^{n_L}
A small truncation measure does not establish the physical adequacy of an active space. Separate finite-bond-dimension error from active-space and basis error.
Assumptions, implementation status and JSON
White, S. R. (1992)
White, S. R.; Martin, R. L. (1999)

records.title: Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations
records.section: Born–Oppenheimer molecular dynamics / BOMD
records.text:
BOMD minimizes electronic energy at each nuclear configuration and integrates nuclear motion with the gradient of the Born–Oppenheimer surface. Energy tolerances and force accuracy are separate criteria; a moving finite basis also contributes position derivatives.
Static DFT convergence does not establish a correct MD trajectory. The separate From DFT to atomic forces chapter independently checks asymmetric-He₂ forces and a BOMD force interface with a short local step comparison. Long NVE drift and systematic trajectory convergence versus timestep and SCF tolerance remain future validation tasks. The periodic-DFT chapter contrasts BOMD with CPMD.
E_{\mathrm{BO}}(\mathbf R)=\min_{\langle\psi_i|\psi_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}}E_{\mathrm{KS}}[\{\psi_i\};\mathbf R],\qquad M_I\ddot{\mathbf R}_I=\mathbf F_I=-\nabla_{\mathbf R_I}E_{\mathrm{BO}}(\mathbf R)
Long equations scroll horizontally.
The existing force release checks a BOMD interface. A separate quantum-small dimensionless two-state BO/CP-type model checks short coupled motion and a nuclear thermostat. General KS first-principles MD, real materials, long trajectories and equilibrium thermostat sampling remain unvalidated.
Assumptions, implementation status and JSON
M. Born; R. Oppenheimer (1927)
R. Car; M. Parrinello (1985)

records.title: Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations
records.section: Car–Parrinello molecular dynamics / CPMD
records.text:
Car–Parrinello dynamics propagates orbitals and nuclei through an extended Lagrangian with fictitious orbital inertia μ and orthonormality constraints. This electronic motion is distinct from real-time TDDFT and physical electronic excitation.
Inspect μ, timestep, orthogonality tolerance and fictitious kinetic energy to maintain proximity to the BO surface. The separate quantum-small release is a short dimensionless two-state CP-type coupled model, not general KS-orbital CPMD. Static periodic-He energy agreement is not CPMD validation.
L_{\mathrm{CP}}=\frac12\sum_I M_I|\dot{\mathbf R}_I|^2+\frac{\mu}{2}\sum_i\langle\dot\psi_i|\dot\psi_i\rangle-E_{\mathrm{KS}}+\sum_{ij}\Lambda_{ij}\bigl(\langle\psi_i|\psi_j\rangle-\delta_{ij}\bigr)
Long equations scroll horizontally.
General KS-orbital CPMD implementation and long-time validation remain unperformed. Short trajectories in the separate two-state educational model do not certify real-material adiabatic separation or long-time energy transfer.
Assumptions, implementation status and JSON
R. Car; M. Parrinello (1985)

records.title: Radiation transport and moment methods
records.section: Radiation transport and moment methods
records.text: Radiation transport resolves intensity in space, direction and frequency. Moment methods reduce the angular dimension but require closure for information removed by integration.

records.title: Radiation transport and moment methods
records.section: Problem and representative equations
records.text:
Use frequency-integrated grey intensity I in a static medium, with isotropic emissivity η and absorption coefficient κ of inverse-length units; omit scattering here. Define E=(1/c)∫I dΩ, F=∫nI dΩ and P=(1/c)∫nnI dΩ. Moment equations for E and F require a prescription for P.
 rac1c\partial_t I+\mathbf n\cdot
abla I=\eta-\kappa I,\qquad\partial_t E+
abla\cdot\mathbf F=4\pi\eta-c\kappa E,\qquad c^{-2}\partial_t\mathbf F+
abla\cdot\mathbf P=-\kappa\mathbf F/c.

records.title: Radiation transport and moment methods
records.section: Algorithm
records.text: Discrete ordinates discretizes angle directly; moment methods close P=D E. M1 obtains D locally from E and F, while flux-limited diffusion instead approximates F from the gradient of E. Check optically thick and free-streaming limits and couple matter exchange through a consistent energy balance.

records.title: Radiation transport and moment methods
records.section: Conditions and pitfalls
records.text:
M1 generally cannot propagate crossing beams independently. FLD ties flux to the energy gradient, limiting shadows and strongly anisotropic fields. A reduced light speed changes transport/relaxation scales and must be justified against the physical time scales of interest.
The companion retains a one-dimensional steady purely absorbing slab with specified inflow, solving μ∂xI=−κI. General radiation moment closures, scattering, time dependence, multiple frequencies and fluid coupling are unvalidated.

records.title: Radiation transport and moment methods
records.section: What to check
records.text:
Test exponential absorption, isotropic diffusion, free streaming/shadows and crossing beams separately. Check E≥0, |F|≤cE, matter-plus-radiation energy and angular/spatial/time convergence. Distinguish closure error from discretization error.
Use directional Beer–Lambert solutions and a continuum-angle exponential integral, separating upwind spatial error at fixed ordinates from angular-quadrature error with exact ray propagation. Check inflow–outflow versus volume absorption and positivity separately; a balance check alone does not establish angular-distribution accuracy.
At optical depths 0.1/0.7/3, cross-check the continuum-angle reference using expn and a separate adaptive QUADPACK quadrature. Independent transport sampling draws μ=√U for the incident flux and counts transmission as a Bernoulli variable. Check binomial intervals and RMSE over 64 finite-sample replicates; nominal 95% coverage is not claimed for arbitrary inputs or samples.

records.title: Euler reconstruction: PPM, characteristics, WENO-Z and AUSM
records.section: Euler reconstruction: PPM, characteristics, WENO-Z and AUSM
records.text:
Open the computed comparison. This 1D experiment separates
reconstruction choices from numerical-flux choices. It extends the original
componentwise MUSCL/WENO baseline; previous exhibits are retained.

records.title: Euler reconstruction: PPM, characteristics, WENO-Z and AUSM
records.section: What is compared#
records.text:
The reconstruction view compares conservative-component and characteristic
MUSCL/MC, limited parabolic finite volumes, and finite-difference WENO5-JS/Z.
FV uses HLLC; FD uses global Lax–Friedrichs flux splitting. Both use SSPRK3,
nominal CFL 0.3 and the same number of grid locations. Their representations,
fluxes and error norms differ: this is not an isolated reconstruction or
matched-cost ranking. Within each method, changing only the basis is a
controlled component/characteristic comparison.
The separate flux view fixes conservative characteristic MUSCL/MC and SSPRK3,
then switches HLLC, acoustic-smoothed Roe, Einfeldt-type HLLE and the explicitly
defined AUSM baseline below. It does not change the spatial reconstruction.

records.title: Euler reconstruction: PPM, characteristics, WENO-Z and AUSM
records.section: Limited parabolic finite volumes#
records.text:
Following the reconstruction idea of Colella–Woodward (1984),
form a parabola in each cell from its mean and two edges. The inspected public
1982 author preprint is an earlier
version, not the final journal layout. This implementation includes limited
edge interpolation and monotonicity constraints, coupled by method of lines
to SSPRK3. It excludes original PPM wave tracing, contact steepening, shock
flattening, Lagrangian evolution and remap. Direct-Eulerian tracing, contact steepening and flattening are now available in the second computed stage; Lagrangian evolution and remap remain future work.
For a cell mean Q and edges L,R, use the local coordinate ξ in [0,1]:
 q(\xi)=L+\xi[R-L+q_6(1-\xi)],\qquad q_6=6Q-3(L+R).
The integral is exactly Q. Limit initial edge interpolation between adjacent
means; flatten a parabolic extremum and apply the usual curvature bounds.
Characteristic projection freezes a local conservative eigenbasis in each
cell, limits projected deviations, then transforms back. Components are
conservative variables, not primitive variables. Reconstructed left/mid/right
states share one affine positivity scaling about Q if needed. Their Simpson
mean remains Q; no conserved mean is clipped. Inadmissible RK stages retry
with a halved time step. These safeguards do not prove fully discrete positivity.

records.title: Euler reconstruction: PPM, characteristics, WENO-Z and AUSM
records.section: Characteristic finite-difference WENO-Z#
records.text:
For each face freeze a Roe-averaged conservative eigenbasis. Project the
positive and negative global-LF split flux stencils, reconstruct each
characteristic component, and transform the resulting face flux back.
FD evolves point values; it is not FV state reconstruction. Shared flux
differences conserve the discrete sum on a periodic grid.
The Z variant uses the JS smoothness indicators with
 \tau_5=|\beta_0-\beta_2|,\quad
 \alpha_k^Z=d_k\left[1+\left(\frac{\tau_5}{\beta_k+\epsilon}\right)^2\right],
 \quad\omega_k^Z=\frac{\alpha_k^Z}{\sum_l\alpha_l^Z},
 \quad(d_0,d_1,d_2)=(0.1,0.6,0.3).
Here ε = 10⁻⁶ is fixed and the Z exponent is 2. These choices must accompany
comparisons; the regularization and normalization of the characteristics affect
the weights. Borges, Carmona, Costa and Don (2008)
is the original bibliographic reference. Publisher metadata and the public
earlier three-author manuscript
were inspected; that manuscript has different weight conventions. The formula
above, its exponent and the executable checks define this edition's variant;
no final-paper figure is reproduced.

records.title: Euler reconstruction: PPM, characteristics, WENO-Z and AUSM
records.section: AUSM: keep the variant explicit#
records.text:
Liou–Steffen (1993) introduced AUSM.
The local baseline uses a common interface sound speed a = (aL+aR)/2,
Mach polynomials M± = ±(M±1)²/4 in the subsonic interval, and the cubic
pressure fractions P± = (M±1)²(2∓M)/4. Supersonic branches use signed upwind
Mach and pressure fractions. These formulas were cross-checked against the
official FEST-3D AUSM source.
This is an independently implemented, specified AUSM-family variant, not
FEST-3D output or a reproduction of every 1993 sound-speed/pressure option.
Let Mf = M+(uL/a)+M−(uR/a). Upwind the advected vector (ρ,ρu,ρv,ρH)
using a max(Mf,0) on the left and a min(Mf,0) on the right, and add
pL P+(uL/a)+pR P−(uR/a) to normal momentum only. Energy transports total
enthalpy. Tests include uniform states, both supersonic directions, Mach ±1
branch limits, stationary/moving contacts and the computed Euler problems.
AUSM+ (1996) and
AUSM+-up (2006) are separately defined in the new traced-PPM comparison. The current baseline has no all-speed correction or low-Mach
verification. None of these names implies universal shock stability; inspect
the separate odd–even comparison.

records.title: Euler reconstruction: PPM, characteristics, WENO-Z and AUSM
records.section: Problems, references and accuracy#
records.text:
Sod: N=200, x∈[0,1], t=0.2, standard states, extrapolated ends.
Moving contact: N=200, periodic [0,1], u=p=1, density 1 on the first
half and 2 on the second; one crossing t=1.
Shu–Osher: N=240, x∈[−5,5], t=1.8, fixed end states, shock at −4,
left (ρ,u,p)=(3.857143,2.629369,10.33333), right density 1+0.2sin(5x), u=0,p=1.
The dashed curve is our internal characteristic FD WENO-Z N=960 run, not
an exact solution or an external-code validation.
FV initialization integrates conserved quantities. Sod final density errors
use 128-node Gauss quadrature of the analytic Riemann solution; the saved
64/128-node discrepancy estimates quadrature sensitivity across discontinuities.
FD errors are pointwise. Derived FV primitive curves are primitive variables
of conserved means, not exact primitive means. No exact Shu–Osher error is reported.
A separate smooth periodic entropy wave uses N=32,64,128 at t=0.2 and
CFL = 0.25(32/N)^(2/3). This reduces dt proportional to dx^(5/3), making the
SSPRK3 time error O(dx⁵). Measured WENO orders are about five on this smooth
case; limited PPM is about two on this sequence because of extremum limiting.
This is not a global fifth-order guarantee at shocks or arbitrary critical points.
Reproduce with python scripts/build_reconstruction.py. Download
profiles, diagnostics and source hashes
and conserved arrays. The final arrays,

records.title: Exact and reference solutions
records.section: Exact and reference solutions
records.text: A verification library should say what its answer means. The reference explorer contains 18 cases with formulas, assumptions, source links, point values and, for one-dimensional cases, cell means. It evaluates references; it does not advance a numerical PDE solution.

records.title: Exact and reference solutions
records.section: Four different reference categories#
records.text:
Analytic: explicit formulas, including scalar entropy waves, sine translation/decay, dry-bed and vacuum fans, channel profiles and Taylor–Green flow. Floating-point evaluation still has rounding error.
Semi-analytic: Euler, wet shallow-water and isothermal Riemann solutions. The wave curves are analytic, but matching the middle state requires a numerical scalar root solve.
Manufactured: prescribe a smooth field and derive the forcing and boundary conditions. The Poisson sine case tests a forced problem chosen for that field.
Numerical reference: a refined numerical computation. It retains discretization, boundary and time-integration errors. Existing high-resolution atlas comparisons belong here when explicitly identified; they are not additional analytic cases in this library.
Agreement with a reference verifies a particular setup. It does not validate a physical model against experiments or certify every boundary treatment.

records.title: Exact and reference solutions
records.section: Included fields and assumptions#
records.text:
The scalar cases are periodic sine advection and heat decay, Burgers shock/fan and quadratic traffic shock/fan. Euler includes Sod, Lax, a double rarefaction and a generated vacuum, all for an ideal gas with gamma 1.4. Shallow water includes a wet dam break, expansion into a dry bed and a dry middle state, with a flat bottom and gravity 1. Isothermal Euler uses constant sound speed 1 and strictly positive initial density; it has no energy equation and no finite vacuum state.
The viscous cases are planar steady Couette and Poiseuille profiles in a unit channel and a periodic two-dimensional Taylor–Green vortex. Channel profiles are velocity fields, not compressible conserved states. Taylor–Green returns velocity and pressure with a fixed zero-mean pressure gauge. The Poisson manufactured sine returns both the field and its forcing.
These are canonical, nondimensional setups. Dry-bed/vacuum support in the reference evaluator does not add that capability to the existing positive-state finite-volume solver. Topography, viscosity in Riemann problems, arbitrary equations of state and multidimensional shock interactions are outside this first library.

records.title: Exact and reference solutions
records.section: Point values and finite-volume means#
records.text:
For a conserved state, a finite-volume comparison uses
\overline{\boldsymbol U}_i(t)=\frac{1}{x_{i+1/2}-x_{i-1/2}}
\int_{x_{i-1/2}}^{x_{i+1/2}}\boldsymbol U(x,t)\,dx.
The library integrates density, momentum and total energy for Euler, and depth/density and momentum for shallow-water/isothermal flow. Converting a mean conserved state to primitive variables is generally different from averaging primitive variables. A shock cutting a cell makes a center sample particularly misleading.
Known shocks, contacts and both edges of rarefaction fans split each integral into smooth pieces. Gauss–Legendre quadrature uses 24 and 48 points per piece; saved means use the 48-point result. The maximum difference between the two orders is a convergence estimate, not a rigorous error bound. This convention also applies to analytic cases: their saved cell means use finite-order quadrature rather than symbolic integration.
For a nonuniform mesh, the reported error norms are normalized by total domain length:
L_1=\frac{\sum_i\Delta x_i|e_i|}{\sum_i\Delta x_i},\qquad
L_2=\left(\frac{\sum_i\Delta x_i e_i^2}{\sum_i\Delta x_i}\right)^{1/2},\qquad
L_\infty=\max_i|e_i|.
Each component is reported separately. The Euler/SWE/isothermal equation gallery now uses these conserved cell means. Its saved physical times still come from independent final-time numerical solves.

records.title: Exact and reference solutions
records.section: Riemann construction and tolerances#
records.text:
The self-similar solution uses xi=(x−x0)/t. For Euler the matched unknown is pressure; for shallow water it is depth; for isothermal flow it is density. The implementation brackets a monotone wave-matching residual in the logarithm of that positive unknown, then bisects. The target logarithmic bracket width is 2e−13, with at most 160 bisections and a final residual check of 2e−10 times a characteristic velocity scale. An exact zero residual can terminate earlier. Iterations, final bracket width and residual are saved alongside each case.
Separating Euler or shallow-water fans can create a middle vacuum/dry region. Those cases bypass the positive-state root solve. Conserved variables vanish there. Velocity is physically undefined in vacuum; the low-level conversion displays zero by convention. Isothermal expansion approaches arbitrarily small positive density instead of a finite vacuum. States outside the supported float64 range raise an error rather than silently clipping the reference.
The Clawpack Euler chapter and shallow-water chapter describe the wave construction and dry/vacuum cases. Bhat and Fetecau's author manuscript gives the isothermal wave curves for the original Euler system in its Riemann-problem discussion; this library uses that original system, not the paper's regularized model.

records.title: Exact and reference solutions
records.section: Viscous and manufactured formulas#
records.text:
For a unit-height channel, unit density and viscosity nu, the steady profiles are
u_{\rm Couette}(y)=y,\qquad
u_{\rm Poiseuille}(y)=\frac{G}{2\nu}y(1-y),\qquad G=1,\quad\nu=0.1.
Couette has wall speeds 0 and 1 with zero pressure gradient. Poiseuille has stationary no-slip walls; G is either the negative pressure gradient per unit density or an equivalent body acceleration. These are fully developed planar flows, not pipe flow.
For Taylor–Green on the periodic square [0,2pi]², with nu=0.1 and unit density,
u=\sin x\cos y\,e^{-2\nu t},\qquad
v=-\cos x\sin y\,e^{-2\nu t},\qquad
p=\frac{\cos(2x)+\cos(2y)}4e^{-4\nu t}.
The Web explorer displays an x-slice at y=pi/4, not two-dimensional area means. The Python evaluator accepts full 2D coordinates and smooth rectangular box averages. Related methods are in the viscous-flow chapter.
The manufactured case prescribes u=sin(pi x), giving −u_xx=f=pi² sin(pi x) with homogeneous Dirichlet endpoints. Its source is available through the same object; it is not an arbitrary-source Poisson solver.

records.title: Exact and reference solutions
records.section: Reuse and reproduce#
records.text:
import numpy as np
from numart.reference_solutions import get_reference, riemann_reference
ref = get_reference('euler-sod')
edges = np.array([0., .15, .42, .51, .7, 1.])
points = ref.point((edges[:-1] + edges[1:]) / 2, t=.2)
report = ref.cell_average_report(edges, t=.2)
means = report['values'] # columns: rho, rho*u, E
# With actual numerical conserved means q of the same shape:
# errors = ref.compare_means(q, edges, t=.2)
custom = riemann_reference('shallow-water', (2., 0.), (1., 0.),
 parameter=9.81)
tg = get_reference('taylor-green')
box_mean = tg.box_average([0., 0.], [.2, .3], t=.5)
Rebuild the saved profiles and figure with MPLCONFIGDIR=.mplconfig python scripts/build_reference_solutions.py. Download the data and numerical source hashes. Python tests compare Euler with an existing independent implementation, check Rankine–Hugoniot jumps and Lax inequalities, rarefaction PDE residuals and invariants, global balances, known integrals, manufactured forcing and Taylor–Green momentum/divergence residuals. The Web build checks the saved schema, wave locations, source hashes and averaging conventions.
Blasius, Sedov, Noh and additional multidimensional references remain future extensions. LANL ExactPack is an independent source collection to consult for those additions; it is not a dependency or a claim of cross-validation for the cases above.

records.title: Relativistic hydrodynamics: SRHD, GRHD, and GRMHD
records.section: Relativistic hydrodynamics: SRHD, GRHD, and GRMHD
records.text:
Literature review, checked 6 November 2026. These methods are not implemented
in the atlas's Newtonian Euler library. The development has several interacting
branches: conservative shock capture, curved and evolving geometry, magnetic
constraints, physical-state recovery, high-order methods, radiation, and
portable parallel computation. Dates below distinguish publication from
preprint and acceptance dates. This is a selected reading path, not an
exhaustive review or a ranking of codes.

records.title: Relativistic hydrodynamics: SRHD, GRHD, and GRMHD
records.section: What changes from the existing Euler examples?#
records.text:
SRHD evolves relativistic matter in flat spacetime. GRHD includes a curved
metric, which may be prescribed or evolved with Einstein's equations. GRMHD
also evolves the electromagnetic contribution. A Kerr-background accretion
calculation and a binary-neutron-star calculation with dynamical spacetime
therefore test different systems.
With c = G = 1 and metric signature (-,+,+,+), ideal-fluid equations are
\nabla_\mu(\rho_0 u^\mu)=0,\qquad
\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0,\qquad
T^{\mu\nu}=\rho_0 h u^\mu u^\nu+p g^{\mu\nu},\qquad
h=1+\epsilon+\frac{p}{\rho_0}.
Here rho0 is rest-mass density and epsilon is specific internal energy. In
Cartesian SRHD, a common conservative state is
W=(1-v^2)^{-1/2},\qquad
D=\rho_0W,\quad S_i=\rho_0hW^2v_i,\quad
\tau=\rho_0hW^2-p-D.
It differs from the Newtonian state in the existing benchmarks.
Primitive recovery is nonlinear. One-dimensional acoustic speeds with zero
transverse velocity are (v +/- cs)/(1 +/- v cs), not v +/- cs. In a 3+1 GR
formulation, lapse, shift, spatial volume factors, and metric derivatives
enter the fluxes and sources. These are structural changes, not a different
value of gamma. Font (2008) is the
formulation review used here; the original Valencia reference is below.

records.title: Relativistic hydrodynamics: SRHD, GRHD, and GRMHD
records.section: 1972–1998: from curved-background flows to conservative HRSC#
records.text:
Wilson (1972)
is an early numerical study of gas falling into a Kerr black hole. It provides
historical context for relativistic fluid computation, rather than a claim
that fixed-background hydrodynamics solves the full evolving Einstein system.
The high-resolution shock-capturing (HRSC) branch brings the characteristic
and conservative methods of classical CFD into relativity.
Martí and Müller (1994)
give an exact SR Riemann solution for flow normal to the initial discontinuity.
That scope matters when selecting multidimensional tests with transverse
velocities; the original normal-flow reference is not a general transverse
Riemann solution.
Banyuls et al. (1997) present the 3+1 local
characteristic formulation commonly called Valencia. Its conservative state,
characteristic information, and geometric source terms make modern shock
capture applicable in GR. It is a central reference, not a claim that all
earlier relativistic methods were nonconservative.
Pons et al. (1998) connect GRHD to SR
Riemann solvers through a local coordinate transformation. Curvature and
coordinate effects still have to be accounted for outside that local solve.

records.title: Relativistic hydrodynamics: SRHD, GRHD, and GRMHD
records.section: 1999–2006: magnetic constraints and dynamical spacetime#
records.text:
Komissarov (1999)
develops a multidimensional Godunov-type relativistic MHD scheme with magnetic
flux conservation. HARM, Gammie–McKinney–Tóth (2003)
combines conservative GRMHD, HLL fluxes, and a Tóth-type CT construction, with
black-hole torus calculations among its examples. Its original formulation
must be distinguished from later dynamical-spacetime frameworks.
Duez et al. (2005) evolve the coupled
Einstein–Maxwell–MHD system, using BSSN for spacetime and conservative shock
capture for the matter. This is the additional step needed when matter and
geometry affect one another dynamically.
Conservation variables do not remove the need to recover physical fluid
states. Noble et al. (2006)
compare nonlinear recovery algorithms, including reductions to one or two
unknowns. Recovery failure, atmosphere floors, and repairs must be tracked
separately from truncation error and conserved-variable residuals.

records.title: Relativistic hydrodynamics: SRHD, GRHD, and GRMHD
records.section: 2011–2026: the particle branch from GSPH#
records.text:
Inutsuka's original GSPH connects to
Iwasaki–Inutsuka (2011), a Newtonian
particle MHD method using Riemann problems and Alfvén characteristics.
It is not itself relativistic.
Kitajima–Inutsuka–Seno (2026)
then formulate special relativistic Godunov SPH (SRGSPH). The paper addresses
convolution-based interactions, unequal baryon numbers, and variable smoothing
lengths, with shock-tube and Kelvin–Helmholtz examples. It is a direct bridge
between the requested particle and relativistic branches. The preprint is
from October 2025; the journal issue is January 2026, despite the DOI's 2025
identifier. It should not be described as a GRHD implementation.

records.title: Relativistic hydrodynamics: SRHD, GRHD, and GRMHD
records.section: 2013 onward: radiation and microphysics add stiff systems#
records.text:
Sądowski et al. (2013) describe KORAL's
covariant M1 radiation moments with semi-implicit interaction sources. This
connects relativistic fluid methods to the atlas's planned implicit and IMEX
chapters. M1 closes angular moments; it does not solve the full radiation
distribution without approximation.
For neutron-star mergers, Foucart (2023)
reviews leakage, moment, and Monte Carlo neutrino transport and the remaining
interaction-modeling limitations. Tabulated finite-temperature equations of
state, composition, transport, and their uncertainties are separate advances
from the choice of a Riemann flux. Ideal relativistic hydrodynamics also does
not automatically supply a causal relativistic viscous theory.

records.title: Relativistic hydrodynamics: SRHD, GRHD, and GRMHD
records.section: A parallel 1979–2019 branch: causal viscous fluid theory#
records.text:
The Newtonian viscous stress cannot simply be
inserted into relativistic Euler equations without examining causality and
the initial-value problem. Israel–Stewart (1979)
provides a central reference for transient dissipative theories with additional
relaxation variables.
Bemfica–Disconzi–Noronha (2019) and
Kovtun (2019) develop a different line:
appropriate first-gradient constitutive choices and hydrodynamic frames can
support causal or stable formulations under specified conditions. The former
paper addresses nonlinear causality without extra extended variables; the
latter examines stable first-order frames. Their results should not be merged
into an unconditional claim for every equation of state or transport choice.
Physical causality, PDE well-posedness, and stability of a discrete time step
are separate checks. This branch is theory and reading context in the atlas,
not an implemented viscous relativistic solver.

records.title: Relativistic hydrodynamics: SRHD, GRHD, and GRMHD
records.section: 2022–2025: high order with shocks, surfaces, and physical constraints#
records.text:
Deppe et al. (2022) develop a DG–finite
difference hybrid: attempt a high-order DG update and recompute inadmissible
regions with robust FD. The 2021 preprint and 2022 publication dates should
remain distinct. Their binary-neutron-star study (2024 preprint)
extends the hybrid approach to dynamical spacetime and merger calculations.
The latter is cited here as a preprint; a separate journal record has not been
verified in this review.
Cao–Peng–Wu (2025)
study physical-constraint-preserving, oscillation-eliminating DG for GRHD,
including positive thermodynamic states and subluminal velocity under their
stated scheme assumptions. Their results are not a guarantee for arbitrary
limiters, fluxes, EOS, or spacetime discretizations. A theorem for a selected
GRHD formulation and an astrophysical merger-code demonstration are different
types of evidence.

records.title: Relativistic hydrodynamics: SRHD, GRHD, and GRMHD
records.section: 2025–2026: portable GPU computation of the coupled system#
records.text:
AthenaK, Fields et al. (2025)
demonstrates dynamical-spacetime GRMHD and binary-neutron-star mergers on GPUs,
with CT and first-order flux correction among its numerical ingredients.
Its preprint is from 2024; the journal reference is ApJS 276, 35 (2025).
AsterX, Kalinani et al. (2025 issue)
provides another open GPU-oriented GRMHD framework, based on Valencia and Z4c.
Its online publication was December 2024. Refinement infrastructure is part
of those source codes; implementing AMR in this atlas remains deferred.
GRACE, Musolino et al.
was accepted by Physical Review D on 2 November 2026, as checked on
6 November. Its July 2026 preprint
describes Kokkos-based portability, CT, Z4c coupling, and neutron-star merger
examples. Acceptance is not a verified final volume/page citation.
These papers establish examples of portable implementations; they do not
establish a universal speed or accuracy ranking across hardware and physics.

records.title: Relativistic hydrodynamics: SRHD, GRHD, and GRMHD
records.section: What the atlas can reproduce in stages#
records.text:
The following is an implementation proposal, not a result of this review:
SRHD: primitive/conservative round trips, characteristic speeds, smooth
waves, shock tubes, reflection, and transverse-velocity cases. Check EOS
validity, rho and pressure positivity, and speeds below c.
SRMHD: add relativistic Alfvén waves, magnetic shock tubes, and a rotor;
specify the magnetic-divergence operator and every repair/floor.
Fixed-metric GR: metric-aware flat-space limits, Michel/Bondi accretion,
equilibrium stars, and torus configurations, with geometric source balance.
Dynamical GR: couple a separately verified spacetime evolution; monitor
Einstein constraints, baryon conservation, stellar oscillations, and waveform
convergence before attempting mergers.
Radiation or SRGSPH: keep each branch's state, boundary, conservation,
transport closure, and reference tests explicit. Reuse the Newtonian examples
as comparisons, not as evidence that a relativistic solver already exists.
The historical conclusion is that progress comes from the combination of
these layers. A new high-order reconstruction or a larger GPU run alone does
not resolve primitive recovery, surface/atmosphere handling, constraint errors,
or microphysical uncertainty.

records.section: v0.1.0 — First edition
records.text:
The first edition of The Art of Numerical Algorithms connects historical
papers with equations, executable educational implementations, benchmark
figures, and numerical verification.

records.title: v0.1.0 — First edition
records.section: Included#
records.text:
An English historical atlas and method notes covering conservation laws, stability, diffusion, boundary conditions, iterative solvers, DG, spectral methods, and MHD.
A Python library and CLI for Euler, shallow-water, isothermal, linear-advection, diffusion, Poisson, and planar ideal-MHD examples.
Godunov-type and MUSCL finite volumes, Rusanov/HLL/HLLE/HLLC/Roe fluxes, FD WENO5-JS, modal DG, and Fourier propagation.
Thomas elimination, matrix-free conjugate gradients, red-black relaxation, and geometric multigrid.
Minimal dual-time, matrix-scaling, and scalar residual-distribution examples.
CT and GLM magnetic-constraint demonstrations with distinct divergence diagnostics.
A 39-entry bibliography with English source notes, generated Markdown and BibTeX, plus a NASA 2D case catalog for future work.
Automated numerical checks and a gallery-generation workflow for Python 3.9 and 3.12.

records.title: v0.1.0 — First edition
records.section: Install and run#
records.text:
Requires Python 3.9 or later. From the repository root:
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install '.[test]'
python -m pytest -q
python -m numart.cli gallery --output outputs/gallery
Start with the reading guide and
benchmark definitions.

records.title: v0.1.0 — First edition
records.section: Scope of this edition#
records.text:
The examples are independently implemented educational models. Their figures
do not claim to reproduce the original papers' figures. Verification covers
selected configurations and does not prove general nonlinear stability or
positivity. Finite-volume and finite-difference errors are identified as
pointwise comparisons, and CT/GLM divergence measurements name their operators.
NASA flow cases, multidimensional Euler rotated-hybrid fluxes, low-Mach PDE
preconditioning, Euler/MHD DG, and multidimensional residual distribution remain
future work. See the roadmap for next steps and the
reference notes for unverified original-source details.

records.title: Implementation roadmap
records.section: Editorial scope
records.text: The focus is mathematical methods, formulations, applicability and verification. AMR (adaptive mesh refinement), parallelization and mixed-precision techniques for computational efficiency are outside the scope of dedicated coverage and development. Ordinary roundoff and numerical stability remain foundational topics.

records.title: Implementation roadmap
records.section: Current development plan and published examples
records.text: Build a development foundation that lets a user’s AI agent obtain implementations, assumptions, benchmark problems and references from the Atlas, then assemble, modify, run and verify code for the requested calculation. Demonstrate this complete development cycle on a few existing-field tasks by year end. Public reproduction, maintenance and restoration support that goal. The 16 December retreat is the first presentation target: an A0 portrait poster, mainly Japanese with English technical terms, reporting the demonstrated results.

records.title: Implementation roadmap
records.section: Current development plan and published examples
records.text: The central year-end deliverable is a prototype in which a user’s AI agent uses public resources and machine-readable manifests to start from Atlas verified implementations, develop the requested code, assess it with Atlas benchmarks and return it to the user. Start with bounded 1D advection and diffusion. Provide bilingual requirements, applicability, retrieval, dependencies, execution, output contracts, references, criteria, failure reasons and citation. Keep original-implementation passes separate from this run’s derived-code receipts. From 22 November 2026, new fields are outside the standard year-end plan. 18 December freezes kit/interface additions and additions to existing validation. Fix reference data, input families and tolerances in advance; agents cannot redefine passing criteria. Quantum chemistry defaults to small educational models, saved-result checks and a few fixed inputs. Large basis/k sweeps, costly independent-reference regeneration, long first-principles MD and precise material calculations require a new explicit request. Development support through users’ existing AI agents is in scope this year; specialist-AI training/model research remains for 2027 or later. records.title: Implementation roadmap
records.section: Target milestones and review gates
records.text:
30 November: select provided code and define the agent contract
Audit existing advection/diffusion code; choose supplied language, dependencies, supported parameters, limits, license and citation. Specify the machine-readable manifest, JSON and array/time/boundary/unit/cell-average contracts, verification CLI and failure reasons for an AI agent to follow request → retrieval → execution → assessment. Distinguish common 22, supplement case/test counts, 83 catalogued problems/39 runnable entrances and 147 methods; synchronize publication status. Preserve old releases, criteria and history; specification is not completed implementation.
12 December: demonstrate code provision through accuracy assessment by a separate AI agent

records.title: Implementation roadmap
records.section: Target milestones and review gates
records.text:
Starting from the public URL and one Japanese and one English calculation request, a separate AI agent completes two advection/diffusion tasks. Record kit retrieval → configuration/implementation modification → execution → reference comparison → error/refinement/invariant assessment → code/report delivery. Fix input families, references and criteria before execution and distinguish original from derived-code results. Use a valid modification and an intentional implementation bug as controls for missing failures or inaccuracy. Check six goal paths; keep this deliverable separate from rerunning original public distributions on existing public inputs. Do not claim success for arbitrary equations, requests or every agent; run no full quantum sweeps. At least one of the two tasks must complete a meaningful source-level assembly/adaptation, such as replacing a spatial operator or time integrator, with an actual diff. Configuration changes alone do not satisfy this gate. Start the demonstration agent with the public URL, request and explicitly listed public materials, without private working copies; record any hints or interventions. By this date, freeze the measured results and distribution/reference/criteria/executed-code versions for the poster, preserving demonstration, intervention and failure records.
16 December: readiness for an A0 portrait poster at the retreat

records.title: Implementation roadmap
records.section: Target milestones and review gates
records.text:
Summarize the two advection/diffusion development demonstrations frozen on the 12th in an A0 portrait poster, mainly Japanese with English terminology. Complete the PDF by the 14th; check full-size readability, figures/equations, citation, QR targets and display/print data on the 15th. Report measured code retrieval → adaptation → execution → accuracy/refinement assessment → artifact delivery, valid/bug controls and original/derived-code distinctions. Keep a demo video and run records locally for explanation without network access. Explicitly show unfinished work, failures, interventions and exclusions; do not prewrite unobserved success. Keep the presentation edition separate from the later year-end candidate and version numerical corrections with reasons.
18 December: freeze provided kits, machine-readable contracts and verification criteria
Pin code, manifests, interfaces, references, input families, criteria and bilingual guidance for the two required tasks by hash, without adding fields. Stop additions to existing validation as well. Carry unfinished P1 extensions forward with reasons and scope; do not relax criteria to meet the date. Limit later work to correctness fixes, explanation and publication checks.
23 December: accept development, verification and delivery in fresh agent contexts

records.title: Implementation roadmap
records.section: Target milestones and review gates
records.text:
Use the frozen candidate in fresh AI-agent contexts to check request → Atlas code retrieval → modification → execution → accuracy/refinement assessment → artifact delivery. Keep original-implementation success, measured derived-code results and failed bug controls in separate receipts. Verify public files, lightweight Linux, bilingual guidance/citation/terms and restoration in another directory. Persist reference/criteria hashes, modification diffs, environment, measured results and CI URL in versioned public evidence. Unresolved P0 prevents completion; do not guarantee arbitrary user requests or code generation across every field. Keep quantum to saved receipts and lightweight fixed examples. At least one of the two tasks must complete a meaningful source-level assembly/adaptation, such as replacing a spatial operator or time integrator, with an actual diff. Configuration changes alone do not satisfy this gate. Start the demonstration agent with the public URL, request and explicitly listed public materials, without private working copies; record any hints or interventions.
31 December: close development-kit corrections and plan the next targets
